books.title: Gems: Treasures from the Earth
books.art_why: Real gems, jewelry, mines, and laboratories can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Many people consider gems to be Earth’s most beautiful creations. They are willing to spend thousands of dollars for even a small bit of that beauty. Sparkling gems are worn on the fingers, necks, and wrists of people around the world. Families pass them down through the years. They can be found on crowns worn by royalty and on sacred religious objects. Many gems decorate the most beautiful and valuable jewelry.
pages.brief: A close view of sparkling gems set in rings, necklaces, and bracelets worn on people's fingers, necks, and wrists. Nearby, an ornate crown and a sacred religious object gleam with jewels. The jewelry looks precious, with family keepsakes and royal and religious pieces shown together.

pages.text: How Are Gems Formed? Some of the most famous and expensive gems, including diamonds, emeralds, and rubies, are crystals. Crystals are very pure forms of minerals. Every mineral is made of millions of tiny particles called atoms. In ordinary rocks, many kinds of atoms are mixed together without any kind of pattern or order. But in crystals, the atoms are arranged very precisely in neat, orderly patterns. Crystals have flat sides, called faces, which form shapes. Different kinds of crystals form in different shapes, some of which are shown below. Some crystals form cubes, while others form long, six-sided columns. TRIGONAL CUBIC TETRAGONAL HEXAGONAL MONOCLINIC Examples of Crystal Shapes.
pages.brief: Several crystals with flat faces in different shapes sit together: cubes, long six-sided columns, and other geometric forms. Inside one crystal, tiny atoms appear in neat, orderly patterns, while ordinary rock nearby shows mixed atoms without any pattern. The crystal faces form clear geometric shapes.

pages.text: VOLCANO Diamonds are formed deep inside Earth’s to the surface. MAGMA LAYERS OF PRESSURE FROM EARTH’S GRAVITY CRUST MANTLE HEAT HEAT DIAMONDS Most crystals form deep within the earth under very special conditions. Some, such as diamonds, form when the mineral is squeezed under layers of rocks. The squeezing forces the atoms to arrange themselves until they are in the smallest shape possible. Others, such as sapphires, form when a mineral gets so hot inside the earth that it melts. As it slowly cools, the atoms fall into place to make a regular crystal pattern. And still other gems, such as opals, form when minerals dissolve in water. As the water evaporates very slowly, the mineral left behind forms a crystal.

pages.text: When a miner finds a gem, it looks very different from the one you see in a ring or necklace. The gem often has rough edges. Its surface looks dull. Its shape is bumpy. Gems often have cracks, dark marks, bubbles, and other flaws. Gem cutters cut gems into regular shapes that show off their best An uncut diamond looks qualities and cover their uneven and flawed. flaws. Gem cutters once used diamond-edged saws and polishers, but recently they began using lasers to cut gems. Most crystal gems are cut into flat surfaces called facets. Facets show off the gem’s color and pattern, and allow it to sparkle with reflected light. Gem cutters cutting styles. A cut diamond reflects lots of sparkle.

pages.text: STEP BRILLIANT CARVING ROSE CABOCHON Cutting styles (top and side views) show gems’ best features. The popular brilliant-cut style is often used with diamonds, which have more sparkle than color. This style has many facets that reflect light off the gem. Deep green emeralds, on the other hand, are often cut into a style called the step cut. This cut, with its rectangular facets, creates a wide, flat top of pure color. The rounded top and triangular facets of another style, the rose cut, are most often found on older gems. The oldest style of cut, the cabochon (KAB-uh-shon), is simply rounded and polished. It is most often used with opaque or patterned stones. Other gems, such as jade and coral, can be carved into small sculptures.

pages.text: What Makes Gems Valuable? Gems as a whole are valuable for two reasons: they are beautiful, and they are rare. The value of a gem is determined by the gem’s hardness and a system called the “four Cs”: cut, carat weight, color, and clarity. Cut refers to how well the gem is cut and polished, or how beautiful the natural gem is. A poorly cut gem may look dull or uneven. Carat weight is the size of the stone. One carat weighs about as much as a kernel of unpopped popcorn. Do You Know? The word carat comes from the seeds of the carob tree. For centuries, jewelers weighed gems according to carob seeds, which grow in pods. The seeds are incredibly similar in weight, no matter which tree or pod they come from. The modern carat weighs about as much as one carob seed.
pages.brief: A jeweler examines a gem, judging its cut and polish, size, color, and clarity. Beside it, a kernel of unpopped popcorn and carob seeds in pods show how carat weight is measured. A poorly cut gem looks dull and uneven, while a well-cut gem appears beautiful and valuable.

pages.text: The next of the four Cs, color, is one of the major reasons why gems are considered beautiful. Unlike regular rocks, gems have bright, pure, strong colors. The stronger and purer the color, the more valuable the gem is. Often, the same mineral can form different-colored gems. Red rubies and blue sapphires both contain the same mineral. The different colors come from tiny bits of other chemicals mixed with the main mineral. It only takes one different atom in a thousand to change the color of a gem. Clarity refers to how flawless the gem is. Gems with dark marks, cracks, and bubbles are less valuable than gems without these flaws. Gems that are cloudy are also less valuable than clearer gems. But clarity is often not as important as the size and rarity of a gem. Emeralds often have many flaws, but because they are so rare, a flawed emerald is more valuable than a flawless diamond. This uncut emerald shows many cracks and other flaws.

pages.text: One of the most famous diamonds, the Hope diamond, is not the largest, but it is a rare sky-blue color. Its long history of theft and ownership by royalty and the rich gave it a legend of being cursed. The largest diamond ever The Hope diamond is one of the most found is the Cullinan famous diamonds in the world. diamond, which was discovered in South Africa. It weighed over 3,100 carats and was as large as a pineapple. It was cut into nine gems, one of which, the Greater Star of Africa, weighs 530 carats. Do You Know? Graphite, or pencil lead, is exactly the same mineral as diamonds. In graphite, the atoms are arranged in loose layers. This makes graphite very soft—so soft that if you rub it on a piece of paper, the atoms break off, leaving a pencil mark. In diamonds, those same atoms have been squeezed together so tightly that nothing except another diamond can scratch them off.

pages.text: The quartz family is the most common of all crystals. Quartz is found all over the world, in all colors of the rainbow. Most quartz is so common that anyone can afford it. The largest quartz crystal ever found was about 6 meters (20 ft) long. It weighed more than 44,000 kilograms (48 tons)— more than a loaded 18-wheeled truck. The most valuable quartz is a multicolored stone called opal. Opals often colors. They in Australia. Quartz crystals are common and can grow very large.

pages.text: Emeralds are known for their green color. Gem-quality emeralds are rare and usually small, but people prize their color so much that emeralds are more valuable than diamonds. The finest emeralds are found in Colombia. The same mineral that forms emeralds also forms a blue- green stone called aquamarine. Jade is one of the most valued stones. It occurs in lavender, white, and almost every shade of green, which is the most valuable. Jade is very tough but easy to carve along its grain. Many civilizations, especially in Asia, used jade to make beautiful knives, swords, and axes. Jade figurine (above); (left)

pages.text: Turquoise is often specked and striped with black. Blue-green turquoise comes from the deserts of Iran, Tibet, and the southwestern United States. This stone often has pretty spots and streaks running through it. Much of the world’s turquoise is set in silver, as the Navajo Native Americans traditionally wore it. The Navajo believed turquoise to be pieces of the sky that had fallen to Earth.
pages.brief: A blue-green turquoise stone, speckled and striped with black, rests in a silver setting. The stone comes from the deserts of Iran, Tibet, and the southwestern United States. Navajo Native Americans traditionally wore turquoise in silver and believed the stones were pieces of the sky that had fallen to Earth.

pages.text: Natural pearls are strangely shaped and are very rare. It takes an oyster many years to create a pearl from a tiny bit of sand. Almost all of the beautiful round pearls in jewelry stores are cultured, or made by people. Pearl farmers place a round shell bead into an oyster’s shell. The oyster covers the bead with nacre, creating a perfectly round pearl. Cultured pearls come in every color of the rainbow, from creamy white to pink to yellow to green and even black. Natural pearls (inset) are rare and oddly shaped; cultured pearls are round.
pages.brief: A natural pearl, oddly shaped and rare, sits beside a perfectly round cultured pearl. An oyster shell shows a tiny bit of sand being covered with nacre over many years. Pearl farmers place a round shell bead inside an oyster, which coats it with nacre. Cultured pearls appear in creamy white, pink, yellow, green, and black.

pages.text: This strip mine clears an immense area of land. Conclusion Beautiful gems can be found around the world. Many gems are symbols of power and wealth. For centuries, people have killed and died for them. In some places, such as West Africa and Colombia, the gem trade is still filled with blood and violence. Mining gems with dynamite and strip mines is often dangerous, damaging both humans and the Earth. Scientists can grow gems in the lab that are identical to the finest natural gems but cost a thousand times less. In the future, created gems might help fill our desire for gemstones’ beauty while preserving Earth and its people.

In a lab, scientists grow gems identical to the finest natural gems at far lower cost, offering a future that preserves Earth and its people.

pages.text: Introduction: What Is Climate Change? What is the weather like today? Is it warm or cold? Sunny or rainy? It’s easy to see what the weather is like on any given day, but what about the climate? Over long periods, there are certain patterns to the weather. These long-term patterns are called climate. Sometimes these patterns change. For example, it was colder in Europe from 1400 to 1800 than it was from 1100 to 1300. That was because the pattern of weather—the climate— changed between these two periods. Many scientists think that the climate is changing again, back to a warmer pattern. They call this change global warming. Some people are concerned that global warming could harm plant and animal communities and human societies. Other people believe there is little to worry about. This book tells what scientists have discovered about climate change. Read it carefully and then ask yourself, “What do I think about climate change?”
pages.brief: A split outdoor scene shows a sunny warm day and a rainy cold day in one neighborhood, while a long European landscape in the background suggests centuries of changing weather; the contrast shows daily weather beside long-term climate patterns.

pages.text: Evidence for Climate Change When scientists have an idea, such as the idea that global warming is happening, they need to present evidence to support that idea. What evidence have scientists discovered about global warming? Meteorologists are scientists who study the weather. They have kept careful records of Earth’s surface temperatures since the mid-1800s. Surface temperatures include the temperature of the air near the ground, such as what you see on an outdoor thermometer. They also include temperatures of the ocean surface. These records show that the average surface temperature around the world has increased by roughly 1.0°F to 1.8°F (0.6°C to 1.0°C) since the late 1800s.
pages.brief: Meteorologists in a weather station examine careful temperature records and an outdoor thermometer near the ground, while a nearby ocean surface is also being measured; the scientists compare long-term surface temperatures from land and sea without any labels or captions.

pages.text: Scientists have also compared records of this recent temperature increase with other evidence of what Earth’s climate was like thousands of years ago. This comparison led a group of U.S. scientists to report in 2006 that Earth’s surface is probably warmer now than at any time in the past twelve thousand years. Old photographs provide other evidence that Earth’s surface is warming. For example, photos of certain mountain glaciers taken in the early to mid-1900s show that the glaciers were larger years ago than they are today. Scientists have found that some of these mountain glaciers are melting and shrinking at faster and faster rates. Scientists have observed such glaciers in Alaska, South America, Europe, and Asia. Many think this shrinking is being caused by an increase in global surface temperatures. Melting glaciers helped cause the Larsen B ice shelf in Antarctica to break into smaller pieces. The ice shelf was four hundred years old.
pages.brief: A mountain glacier is shown as it looked in an old photograph beside the same glacier today, smaller and melting, while in Antarctica the Larsen B ice shelf cracks and breaks into smaller pieces; the cold landscape shows shrinking ice and melting glaciers.

pages.text: Evidence indicates that ice around the North and South Poles is also melting. Much of this evidence comes from photographs of the polar regions taken by cameras on satellites. Satellite photos have shown that the amount of sea ice in the Arctic Ocean around the North Pole has decreased since the 1970s. Measurements revealed that, between 2004 and 2005, an area of sea ice the size of Texas disappeared from the Arctic. Because of the melting Arctic ocean ice, the survival of polar bears may be at risk. Polar bears use ice floes (floating ice) in winter as platforms to hunt seals. Scientists reported in 2005 that there are fewer ice floes in the Arctic Sea than there used to be. As a result, many polar bears are not getting enough to eat. Some may be drowning.
pages.brief: A polar bear stands on a small Arctic ice floe, hunting for seals in a cold sea where fewer ice platforms remain; nearby an iceberg calves into the water, and satellite cameras far above view the shrinking sea ice around the North Pole.

pages.text: Near the South Pole, satellite photos show that both sea ice and ice sheets (ice covering land) in western Antarctica are melting. In 2002, photos showed an ice shelf larger in area than Rhode Island breaking into small pieces and drifting away from Antarctica. An ice shelf is part of an ice sheet that extends into the sea. When ice on land, such as on Antarctica and Greenland, melts, the meltwater flows into the ocean. Over time, this extra water could cause sea levels to rise. Scientists with the United Nations have reported that the average sea level around the world has risen by at least 4 inches (10 cm) since the early 1900s. Searching for More Evidence More evidence for global warming exists than is described in this chapter. Other evidence pointed to by scientists includes: • changes in migration habits of certain birds • an unhealthy condition of coral reefs called “bleaching” • possible increases in extreme weather, such as hurricanes You can find out more about this evidence by using the Internet. However, you need to be careful about which websites you use. Many websites about global warming contain incorrect information. Websites run by government agencies, universities, or scientific organizations are usually the best. When you read about any evidence, remember to ask yourself, “Does this make sense to me? ”
pages.brief: A satellite view of western Antarctica shows an ice shelf breaking into small pieces and drifting away from the frozen coast; meltwater flows toward the ocean, and a simple measuring scene suggests slowly rising sea levels around the world.

pages.text: What Is Causing Climate Change? There are many ideas as to what may be causing global warming and climate change. These ideas can be divided into two main categories: human activities and natural causes. The main human activity blamed for global warming is the burning of fossil fuels —coal, oil, and natural gas. They are used in automobiles, factories, and electric power plants. When they are burned for fuel or energy, carbon dioxide gas and other gases are released into the atmosphere (air). These gases build up in the atmosphere over time. The gases let much of the energy of sunlight pass through the air to warm Earth’s surface. Earth’s surface then radiates (sends out) heat energy back into the air. Much of this heat energy drifts off into space. However, some is trapped near Earth’s surface by carbon dioxide and certain other gases in the atmosphere. The trapped heat energy is then directed back to the surface, warming the surface more. This process acts like a greenhouse—a building in which special glass walls trap heat to warm plants inside. For this reason, it is called the greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide, methane, and other gases that trap heat are called greenhouse gases.
pages.brief: A factory, automobiles and an electric power plant burn coal, oil and natural gas, sending gases into the air; beside them, a glass greenhouse traps warmth around plants, showing how carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases trap heat near Earth’s surface.

pages.text: Greenhouse Gas Sources Carbon dioxide Fossil fuels, burning and cutting down forests, volcanoes Methane Burning forests, microbes in wetlands and inside cattle intestines Nitrous oxide Fossil fuels, burning forests, chemical reactions in soil and ocean Halocarbons Old spray cans, certain cleaning fluids, other products Aerosol particles Fossil fuels, burning forests, volcanoes Ozone Automobiles, power plants Water vapor Evaporation, plants The greenhouse effect is a natural part of how Earth functions. If it did not exist, Earth would be as cold as Mars—too cold for liquid water or life. However, many scientists think that the carbon dioxide released into the air by the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the warming of the greenhouse effect.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor scene shows several sources of greenhouse gases at once: fossil fuels burning at a power plant, a forest being cut and burned, a smoking volcano, cattle in a wetland, old spray cans and cleaning fluids, automobiles, and water vapor rising from plants and water.

pages.text: What is the evidence that carbon dioxide from fossil fuels is related to global warming? Humans began burning fossil fuels in large amounts when industrialization (the use of power-driven machinery) became widespread in the mid-1800s. Since then, measurements suggest that the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased by about 25 percent. According to meteorologists, Earth’s surface temperature has increased during this same time. Deforestation—the cutting down of forests— is another human activity that has increased the carbon dioxide in the air. Trees and other plants remove carbon dioxide from the air. They use it to carry out photosynthesis —the chemical process by which plants make their own food. When there are fewer plants to carry out photosynthesis, more carbon dioxide builds up in the atmosphere.
pages.brief: A mid-1800s industrial scene with power-driven machinery and factories burning fossil fuels, while a modern measurement scene suggests more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere; nearby, people cut down a forest, and leafy plants use carbon dioxide in sunlight to carry out photosynthesis.

pages.text: Some scientists point out that global warming does not have to be caused by human activities. Global warming and global cooling happened over and over before people started burning fossil fuels. During the past few hundreds of thousands of years, there have been several ice ages, when much of Earth’s surface was covered by ice. In between these ice ages have been warm periods. The last ice age ended about 11,500 years ago. According to geologists, we are now in a warm period between two ice ages. What else do weather records and other scientific evidence show? In Europe, the climate cooled between the “Medieval Warm Period” (about 1100 to 1300) and the “Little Ice Age” (about 1400 to 1800). The climate has been warming since the end of the Little Ice Age. These earlier climate changes had natural causes. Perhaps the current global warming has some natural causes, too.
pages.brief: A wide prehistoric landscape shows ice sheets covering much of the land during an ice age, with a warmer green period between ice ages; in the distance, a European town moves from the Medieval Warm Period into the colder Little Ice Age, then toward a warmer present.

pages.text: Meteorologists have only been keeping careful records of Earth’s temperatures since the mid-1800s. So how can we know what earlier temperatures and climates were like? One way to know is by studying the growth rings of very old trees. Trees grow more when the climate is wet and warm than when it is dry and cold. Tree rings are thicker when there is greater growth. By analyzing such rings, scientists can discover trends in temperature going back hundreds of years. To discover even older temperature trends, scientists use various other methods. One such method is to examine ice cores. Ice cores are long samples of ice that are shaped like cylinders. They are drilled out of the ground in Antarctica and other frozen places. An ice core contains chemical evidence A library of ice cores.
pages.brief: Scientists study the thick growth rings of a very old tree and then examine long cylindrical ice cores drilled from frozen ground in Antarctica; deeper ice layers lie below the surface, and the icy samples show chemical evidence of older atmospheres without any labels.

pages.text: Scientists examine an ice core. It shows volcanic activity under a glacier. of what the atmosphere was like during different times. They go back many thousands of years. The deeper the ice, the further back in time it was formed. Certain chemicals, such as large amounts of carbon dioxide, tell scientists that Earth’s climate was relatively warm at the time the ice formed. Such methods allow scientists to learn about Earth’s past natural changes in climate. Although scientists do not fully understand the natural causes of climate change, they suspect that a number of factors are involved. For example, the amount of heat energy produced by the Sun varies from time to time. The shape of Earth’s orbit around the Sun also changes. So does the angle of the tilt that Earth makes on its axis (the imaginary line about which Earth spins).
pages.brief: Scientists examine a long ice core sample that contains ash and chemical traces of volcanic activity under a glacier; the core is layered from top to bottom, deeper layers older, while in the sky the Sun and Earth’s tilted orbit suggest natural factors that change climate over time.

pages.text: Possible Results of Climate Change Whether global warming is caused by human activities, natural factors, or a combination of both, it may result in certain changes to the planet. How do scientists predict these changes? What might these changes be? What would such changes mean to you? Scientists often use computer models to try to predict the future of climate change. These are computer programs based on mathematical equations. They take into account sunlight, heat, rainfall, wind, ocean currents, and other climate factors. Scientists change these equations in different ways to mimic the ways that these factors might change in the real world. The computer program then figures out the most likely effects that these factors would have on Earth’s climate. Computer models are most useful for helping scientists learn several possible results of climate change. However, predictions made with computer models are not certain. These predictions may really happen, but perhaps they won’t. The following possibilities are based on computer models predicting very serious effects of global warming. Other computer models predict far less serious effects.
pages.brief: Scientists sit before computer models built from mathematical equations, with sunlight, heat, rainfall, wind and ocean currents represented in the simulation; the screen shows several possible climate outcomes, and the scientists look closely, knowing the predictions are uncertain.

pages.text: According to some computer models—if current rates of warming continue—Earth’s average surface temperature may increase by as much as 10°F (5.5°C) by 2100. Such a great rise in temperature could cause enormous changes in the natural habitats of many plant and animal species. Wetlands might change into grasslands, and grasslands might change into deserts. Plants and animals that could not adjust to these changes would die out. Large increases in Earth’s surface temperature could cause vast amounts of ice on Antarctica and Greenland to melt into the sea. This could result in sea levels rising several feet. According to some computer models, if all the ice on Greenland were to melt, for example, sea levels might increase by more than 20 feet (6 m). An Inconvenient Truth In 2007, former U.S. Vice President Al Gore was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work in warning the public about the possible dangers of global warming. Gore also wrote a book and appeared in a movie about global warming, both of which were titled An Inconvenient Truth. The book and movie featured several possible disasters that might be in store for Earth because of global warming. These disasters included the extinction of many species of animals, deadly floods in many countries, and much more powerful hurricanes. It is important to keep in mind that these disasters are not definitely going to happen. They are only the worst among many different possibilities.
pages.brief: A computer model shows Earth’s surface growing warmer by 2100, with wetlands turning to grasslands and grasslands to desert; polar ice melts into the sea and sea levels rise, while former U.S. Vice President Al Gore stands beside a book and movie about global warming.

pages.text: If sea levels were to rise high enough and fast enough, many cities along coasts and on small islands would be flooded by ocean water and destroyed. These cities might include New York City, Boston, and other large U.S. cities with millions of people. Earth’s surface temperature affects the weather in many complex ways. Computer models predict that weather in different parts of the world would be affected by continued warming in different ways. In some areas, it could become drier and more difficult to grow crops. This would lead to water and food shortages. In other areas, the growing season could lengthen because of warmer, wetter weather. Crops in these areas would become easier to grow. Changing weather caused by global warming might also mean more hurricanes, tornadoes, snowstorms, or droughts—depending on where a person lives.
pages.brief: Ocean water floods low-lying streets in a large coastal city with tall buildings, while in another region dry fields struggle to grow crops; farther away, a longer growing season brings greener farmland, showing how continued warming could affect different places in different ways.

pages.text: Warmer weather could mean more disease. Many kinds of viruses, bacteria, and other germs spread more easily when the weather is warm than when it is cool. Among such diseases are malaria, dengue (a disease that causes fever and pain), and lung infections. How Global Warming Might Affect You • You might have to conserve electricity, such as by watching less television and using the computer less often. • You might have to deal with more tornadoes, hurricanes, heat waves, and other dangerous weather. • You might experience water or food shortages. • You might be at increased risk of getting certain diseases. • You might find that wild animals you enjoy seeing, such as certain birds and butterflies, become less common.
pages.brief: A warm scene shows germs spreading more easily, with mosquitoes and a sick child representing malaria, dengue and lung infections; nearby, a family conserves electricity by turning off a television and computer, while dangerous weather and fewer wild birds and butterflies appear outside.

pages.text: What Is Being Done About Climate Change? Climate change may have serious effects on human society and wildlife habitats. For this reason, governments around the world are working on this problem. They have come up with plans to limit the possible effects of global warming. Governments of most countries support a plan to limit global warming called the Kyoto Protocol. This plan is named after the city in Japan where the first version of it was written in 1997. According to the plan, industrialized countries will reduce the amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released by power plants, automobiles, and other sources. Industrialized countries are nations with widespread use of machinery and fossil fuels. The greenhouse gas reductions have to be great enough to reach certain levels by certain dates, depending on the country. An Indonesian student plants a tree as part of a climate conference campaign.
pages.brief: Government officials from many countries meet to support the Kyoto Protocol in Japan, where the plan was first written in 1997; in a separate outdoor scene, an Indonesian student kneels in the soil and plants a young tree as part of a climate conference campaign.

pages.text: As of 2010, the government of the United States had not approved the Kyoto Protocol. Some officials in the U.S. government were concerned that the Kyoto Protocol might harm the U.S. economy. Both the federal government and state governments in the United States are working to reduce emissions (releases) of greenhouse gases in other ways. For example, some laws require power plants and factories to reduce their carbon dioxide emissions, such as by using “scrubbers.” Scrubbers are filtering systems that trap carbon dioxide or other pollutants before they are released into the air. Certain newer systems can then store the carbon dioxide underground. Other laws require that automobiles emit less carbon dioxide. Some U.S. factories have reduced the amount of greenhouse gases they emit. Others have not.
pages.brief: U.S. government officials discuss the Kyoto Protocol and economic concerns while a power plant and factory use filtering scrubbers to trap carbon dioxide before release; nearby, carbon dioxide is stored underground, and newer automobiles produce less exhaust, while some factories still emit more than others.

pages.text: The U.S. government also awards money to scientists to help them study “renewable” ways of producing energy. Most renewable energy sources do not use fossil fuels or emit greenhouse gases. They are called renewable, because— unlike fossil fuels— their supplies will not eventually run out. Maple Ridge Wind Farm in New York produces enough energy to power about 160,000 homes. Renewable energy sources include hydropower and geothermal, wind, and solar power. Hydropower uses moving water, such as a river, to produce energy. Geothermal power uses hot water or steam from inside the ground. Wind power uses moving air. Solar power uses sunlight. Nuclear power is another way to produce energy that does not emit greenhouse gases. However, nuclear power produces dangerous wastes. Besides cutting emissions of greenhouse gases, we can also remove some greenhouse gases from the atmosphere. The best way to do this is by planting more trees.
pages.brief: A wide renewable-energy landscape shows a wind farm on a ridge, a hydropower dam with moving water, geothermal steam rising from the ground, and solar panels in sunlight; nearby, people plant trees to remove greenhouse gases, while a separate nuclear plant stands apart because it produces dangerous wastes.

pages.text: Conclusion: What Do You Think? Now that you know what scientists have discovered about climate change and global warming, it’s time for you to think for yourself. What do you think about climate change? How would you answer the following questions? What evidence can you give to support your answers? • Is Earth becoming warmer? • If so, why is Earth becoming warmer? • Could there be more than one reason why the planet is warming? • What might be some results of global warming for plants, animals, and humans? Which results do you think are most likely and least likely? • What, if anything, should be done about climate change? • Will you change your behavior in any way to help reduce climate change? If so, in what ways? • How will you find out more about climate change? Ways You Can Fight Global Warming Less use of fossil fuels equals less release of greenhouse gases. You can reduce your use of fossil fuels by: • Using less electricity • Recycling aluminum cans, paper, and plastics • Walking or riding your bicycle to places that you have to go • Using solar-powered electronic products, such as calculators and watches • Planting trees and gardens.
pages.brief: A thoughtful child sits with an open question in mind, surrounded by everyday choices that reduce fossil fuel use: turning off electricity, recycling cans and paper, walking and riding a bicycle, using a solar calculator and watch, and planting trees in a garden.

books.title: Living in Deserts
books.art_why: Modern deserts, communities, and real people can be photographed today.

pages.text: Bedouin friends embrace in the Sahara in Morocco.
pages.brief: Two Bedouin friends embrace in the Sahara in Morocco. They stand together outdoors in the desert, sharing a warm greeting. The scene places the friends in a wide North African desert setting, with sand around them.

pages.text: A Tuareg woman prepares a meal outside her home in the Sahara in Mali. Demanding Deserts Dictionary definitions of the word desert typically describe barren lands that can support little to no life. While that definition describes some desert regions, other desert landscapes are very different. They include trees, shrubs, and cacti growing on mountainsides. Many kinds of creatures call these areas home. Other deserts appear to be endless seas of sand with waves of rolling sand dunes. Streams and rivers even pass through some desert regions, although the waterways can remain empty for long periods of time.
pages.brief: A Tuareg woman prepares a meal outside her home in the Sahara in Mali. She works outdoors in a desert setting, focusing on the food she is making near her home. The scene shows daily life in a Saharan community.

pages.text: Children run together in India’s Thar Desert. Nearly one-fifth of Earth’s land is deserts. Five of the seven continents have hot deserts (Europe and Antarctica do not). Deserts also vary in size. Some deserts are small, but others are huge. Let’s travel around the world and learn more about some of the world’s deserts and the Indigenous peoples who have called them home for thousands of years. People who live in the desert survive just like everyone else—by adapting to their surroundings. They locate food, water, and shelter as in any other demanding location on Earth. For inhabitants of desert regions, though, the desert isn’t just about survival. It is so much more than that—it is home and a way of life.
pages.brief: A group of children run together in India’s Thar Desert. They move across the desert landscape as a group, playing and running in the open. The scene shows young people enjoying themselves in a hot desert environment.

pages.text: The Tohono O’odham and the Sonoran Desert The hot, dry Sonoran Desert stretches for 310,800 square kilometers (120,000 sq. mi.) across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Months may pass without any rain, and summer days can reach 49º Celsius (120ºF). On the other hand, winter nights can dip below freezing. It rains more in the Sonoran Desert than in any other desert in the world. Summer monsoons often drench the entire desert. Shade trees, large cacti such as the saguaro (suh-WAR-oh), and even summer flowers all grow there. The Tohono O’odham (toe-HOE-noh OH-eh- dom) are Indigenous people who live in the Sonoran Desert. Tohono O’odham means “desert people.” The Sonoran Desert California Arizona New PACIFIC Mexico OCEAN Mexico NORTH NORTH AMERICA AMERICA More than 2,500 native plants grow in the Sonoran Desert. No other desert in the world has more.
pages.brief: The Sonoran Desert stretches across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Large saguaro cacti, shade trees, and summer flowers grow in this hot, dry landscape, where months may pass without rain. The Tohono O’odham live in this desert region.

pages.text: For the past few hundred years, people from Europe and the United States have moved onto and slowly taken land that the O’odham lived on for thousands of years. Today, the land where many O’odham live is divided among four tribes, one of which is the Tohono O’odham Nation. O’odham people at the Gila River Indian Community, the Ak-Chin Indian Community, and the Salt River (Pima Maricopa) Indian Community speak the O’odham language, although there are differences from tribe to tribe. The largest the capital of the Tohono O’odham Nation, is in Sells, Arizona. Today, O’odham people live on and cities. Francine Jose shows baskets made by her relatives long ago.
pages.brief: Francine Jose shows baskets made by her relatives long ago. She presents the baskets in a setting connected to the Tohono O’odham Nation, whose capital is in Sells, Arizona. The scene highlights O’odham traditions kept today.

pages.text: For thousands of years, the desert has provided the O’odham with water, food, and shelter. Using floodwater irrigation techniques, such as water diversion, and carefully selecting planting sites, O’odham became masters at dryland agriculture, growing crops such as corn, squash, and beans. Over time, more of their land was taken and they were pressured by the U.S. government to adapt to the ways of the United States. Still, the O’odham people have fought to keep their traditions over the years. Many O’odham include their traditions in their modern lives, including farming, cooking, and basketmaking. Saguaro Fruit Harvesting The saguaro cactus is an important part of Tohono O’odham culture. Each spring, beautiful flowers bloom on the cactus. Large red fruit then ripens in mid-June. The Tohono O’odham use special tools to harvest the fruit from the tops of the giant cacti, which can reach upwards of 22 meters (75 ft.). They turn the fruit into wine that is important to their New Year celebration in early July.
pages.brief: Tohono O’odham people use special tools to harvest ripe red fruit from the tops of giant saguaro cacti. The cacti can reach upwards of 22 meters, and beautiful flowers bloom before the fruit ripens in mid-June. The harvest is important to their New Year celebration.

pages.text: Bedouin children prepare to race their camels. The Bedouin and the Sahara The Sahara stretches across northern Africa for 8.6 million square kilometers (3.3 million sq. mi.). It is very hot and dry in the Sahara. Because so little rain falls there, few plants and animals flourish there. Bedouin (BED-oo-in) are people who live in the Sahara. Bedouin comes from the Arabic word Badw, which means “people of the desert.” The Sahara Desert Morocco Tunisia Western Sahara Algeria Libya Egypt Mauritania Mali Niger Chad Sudan EUROPE EUROPE ATLANTIC AFRICA OCEAN In some parts of the Sahara, it rains less than AFRICA AFRICA 25 millimeters (1 in.) per year!
pages.brief: Bedouin children prepare to race their camels in the Sahara. The children get ready with their camels in the hot, dry desert, where very little rain falls and few plants and animals flourish. The scene shows a Bedouin tradition in northern Africa.

pages.text: Homes in this Bedouin village in Egypt’s Sahara are built with dry vegetation (top). The inside of this Bedouin tent in Oman is colorful (bottom). Traditionally, the Bedouin are animal herders who roamed the desert during the rainy winter, returning with their camels, sheep, and goats to farmland during the dry summer months. Sparse natural resources forced the Bedouin to be nomadic. They traveled from oasis to oasis and also dug wells to get water. Some Bedouin still live as their ancestors did, but nomadic Bedouin today can also get supplies from markets, sellers, or other places.
pages.brief: Homes in a Bedouin village in Egypt’s Sahara are built with dry vegetation. Inside a Bedouin tent in Oman, colorful materials fill the space. Traditionally, Bedouin herders roamed the desert with camels, sheep, and goats and returned to farmland in dry summer months.

pages.text: Bedouin lived in low black tents, called bayts, made out of goat hair or sheep’s wool. Bayts protected them from the sun, wind, and blowing sand. Some Bedouin still live in them today. In a matter of hours, Bedouins can take down their bayts and pack up their camps. For the past hundred years or so, different countries have been taking over the land where Bedouins have traditionally lived. Many Bedouin are no longer nomadic. Instead, they lead seminomadic or even settled lives. Bedouins no longer only work herding animals. Today, they have many different types of jobs. Umm Sayhoun is a Bedouin village near Petra, in Jordan (left). A Bedouin mother smiles with her son inside their home in Oman (right).
pages.brief: A Bedouin mother smiles with her son inside their home in Oman. A Bedouin village called Umm Sayhoun sits near Petra in Jordan, showing settled life. Low black tents called bayts, made from goat hair or sheep’s wool, once protected Bedouin from sun, wind, and blowing sand.

pages.text: The Gobi Desert ASIA ASIA INDIAN Mongolia OCEAN China The Gobi is a rain shadow desert. It formed because mountains blocked rainy weather that would have allowed plants to flourish there. Mongolian Nomads and the Gobi Stretching for 1.3 million square kilometers (500,000 sq. mi.) across southern Mongolia to the Gobi is a rocky landscape. In the language of the Indigenous Mongolian people, Gobi means “large and dry” or the “waterless place.” Mongolian nomads have been roaming the cold, windy Gobi herding horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and two-humped Bactrian camels for A Mongolian woman herds her animals thousands of years. in the Gobi.
pages.brief: A Mongolian woman herds her animals in the Gobi, a rocky desert stretching across southern Mongolia and China. Mongolian nomads have roamed this cold, windy landscape for thousands of years, herding horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and two-humped Bactrian camels.

pages.text: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family’s ger in the Gobi. Traditionally, home is a yurt—a round tent called a ger. Made of a wooden framework covered in felt, it is able to withstand harsh weather. Gers do a good job of protecting people from extreme heat and cold, but their animals can still suffer. Many families have left nomadic lives in the desert behind. Exceptionally harsh winters and dry summers have caused thousands of families to lose part or all of their herds. Changes in government have also affected herders, making it difficult for them to earn a living. In fact, since 1989, more than half a million Mongolian nomads have moved to Mongolia’s capital city in search of food and work. Most bring their gers with them, leading to districts of gers in the city.
pages.brief: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family’s ger in the Gobi. The round tent, made of a wooden framework covered in felt, stands in the harsh desert weather. Many Mongolian nomads have moved to the capital city and brought their gers with them.

pages.text: A Way of Life People have called deserts home for thousands of years. Each desert has different challenges. The Indigenous peoples who live there have always found solutions using local resources to build homes and find food and water. Today, much has changed, and many desert dwellers lead modern lives. However, some continue to live traditional lives, as their ancestors once did, and many continue to celebrate the traditions of their desert communities. Life in the desert is as demanding as it is rewarding. The people who make the desert their home have always had deep respect for their surroundings. They honor and use its offerings while also recognizing its great power and beauty. A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates.
pages.brief: A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates. The scene shows how desert traditions continue in modern life. People have called deserts home for thousands of years, using local resources to build homes and find food and water.

books.title: The Great Hunger
books.art_why: The Great Hunger is an 1840s event no camera could record, and the book is not about one named famous person, so period drawings fit.

pages.text: United Kingdom United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Ireland Today During the Great Hunger Ireland Great Britain Europe.
pages.brief: Two maps drawn side by side: one shows the island of Ireland beside Great Britain within Europe, the other shows Ireland as it stands today. Green landmasses sit in a blue sea, with the smaller islands of the British Isles scattered around them.

pages.text: Liffey River Bridge, a popular tourist area of Dublin, Ireland The Emerald Isle Ireland, known as the Emerald Isle, is a beautiful island off northwestern Europe with rolling green hills, ancient castles, and windy shores. It has a colorful history and is famous for music, literature, and folklore. Some think of it as a magical land of elves, leprechauns, and faeries. Beyond its natural beauty, Ireland is a hardworking country whose economic health matches that of most of Western Europe. Tourism remains a prime industry. Over six million people travel to Ireland each year to see the beautiful countryside and places of historical interest. It hasn’t always been that way, however.
pages.brief: A drawn view of Dublin's Liffey River Bridge on a bright day, tourists strolling across it. Behind rise rolling green hills, an ancient stone castle and a windy shore. A fiddle and harp lean against a pile of books, standing for music, literature and folklore.

pages.text: A Horrible Discovery Farmers made a horrible discovery as they went to their fields on a foggy, fall day in 1845. The smell of decay filled the air, and the leaves of the potato plants were black and wilted. The farmers dug desperately beneath the plants, only to discover that the potatoes were mushy. Something had the night. Some thought it was the unusually wet, cool weather that had killed the potatoes. Others claimed it must have been tribes of warring faeries A mushy, blackened potato destroyed by a potato blight that had destroyed the crop. Some British people of the Protestant faith thought it was God’s punishment on the Irish people for their Catholic faith. Voyage of the Potato People often associate potatoes with Ireland, but the plant was originally grown in South America. The Spanish brought potatoes to Europe in the 1500s.
pages.brief: On a foggy autumn day in 1845, farmers kneel in a potato field, digging desperately beneath plants whose leaves are black and wilted. Their faces are stricken as they lift out soft, mushy, blackened potatoes. Mist hangs over the dark ridges of soil.

pages.text: People depended on the potato crop for food; three million Irish people ate almost nothing but potatoes. A farmer with an acre of land could grow enough potatoes to feed his family. Potatoes, which could be stored all winter, provided a nutritious diet when eaten with milk, cabbage, and fish. Now a third of the crop rotted in the ground, and struggling families worried about how they would survive until spring.
pages.brief: A farmer stands beside a small potato plot, an acre of ground that once fed his family. Inside a cottage, a family eats potatoes with milk, cabbage and fish. Outside, a third of the crop lies rotted and black in the earth.

pages.text: First Winter The landlords took the farmers’ grain as payment for rent. Without potatoes, families had little to eat. They sold their livestock, furniture, and clothes to buy food. The government opened large workhouses where desperate families could live in exchange for work. No one wanted to go to a workhouse for help. Families worked long hours for a ragged bed and a little food, and no one could leave without permission.
pages.brief: A landlord's agent loads sacks of grain onto a cart while a farming family watches helplessly. Nearby the family sells a cow, a chair and clothes to buy food. In the distance a large grey workhouse stands, families queuing at its gate.

pages.text: The government bought Indian corn from America to help feed the hungry population, but people did not have a way to grind the hard, dry kernels into cornmeal, and some got sick from eating poorly cooked corn. Food got more expensive, and people became desperate to find a way to earn money. The government started public works projects, such as building roads and bridges to provide jobs. The work was hard, and the pay was low. It took nearly five days of work to buy cornmeal to feed a family of six for three days. Still, men walked many miles and stood in long lines to get any work they could find.
pages.brief: Men walk miles along a muddy road and stand in long lines hoping for work. Others labour on a stone road and bridge, breaking rocks for low pay. In a yard, people struggle to grind hard yellow kernels of Indian corn into cornmeal without a mill.

pages.text: Hope, Disaster, and Relief Finally the long winter ended, and farmers eagerly waited for the new potato crop. Disaster struck again in August, when three-fourths of the crop failed. Desperate families had nothing left to sell, the workhouses were crowded, and a long winter with no food loomed ahead. Families like ten-year-old Michael O’Kane’s had no choice but to go to the workhouse because his father, a farm laborer, could find no work. Michael, his parents, two brothers, and three sisters walked hours to the workhouse from Killylea (kih-lee-LAY) Village in September of 1847. He had to live with the boys and men in a separate area away from his mother and sisters. He went to school in the morning and then whitewashed walls or cleaned pigpens all afternoon. His youngest sister, Bridget, died over the winter. Diseases spread easily, especially in the workhouses. Even more people died of typhus and cholera than died of starvation. Despite the obvious need, many officials and landowners in Britain ignored all pleas for help or relief plans. Grain was exported to other countries rather than kept to help Irish farmers.
pages.brief: Ten-year-old Michael O'Kane walks for hours with his parents, two brothers and three sisters from Killylea village to the workhouse in September 1847. Inside he is housed away from his mother and sisters, then whitewashes walls and cleans pigpens all afternoon.

pages.text: Other people wanted to help. The British Relief Association and the Society of Friends (Quakers) raised money for relief. Irish immigrants in America sent money to help family and friends. Soup kitchens opened, and each day up to three million men, women, and children stood outside in long lines for a bowl of soup and a piece of bread. It was not nearly enough.
pages.brief: People queue outside a soup kitchen, a long line stretching down the street. Volunteers ladle soup into bowls and hand out pieces of bread to men, women and children wrapped in thin shawls and worn coats.

pages.text: Going to America Every penny a family had was spent for food, so there was nothing left to pay the overdue rent on their farm. Some landlords gave money or grain to their starving tenants, but it was only a temporary help. Other landowners evicted families from their homes, then tore down or burned the empty houses to avoid paying taxes on them. Driven from their country by hopeless conditions, hundreds of thousands of Irish people crowded onto ships bound for the United States or Canada, leaving their Irish homeland forever.
pages.brief: Landlord's men tear down a cottage roof and burn an empty house while an evicted family stands on the road with their few belongings. In the distance hundreds of people crowd onto a wooden sailing ship bound for America or Canada, leaving Ireland forever.

pages.text: It was a difficult journey because a ship took forty days to cross the Atlantic Ocean, even when the weather was good. Many of the ships carrying the Irish emigrants were called “coffin” ships. Passengers were packed below deck, where disease spread in the overcrowded, filthy conditions. There often was not enough food, water, or blankets for the passengers. Many died, and many of those who survived arrived in America sick and weak. Ireland’s Potato Blight and Famine 1800 to 1840s - POPULATION INCREASE Ireland’s population soars by 50% between 1800 and 1840, but employment remains limited. Struggling rural families depend on potatoes as their main food source. 1845 - FIRST BLIGHT REPORTED IN AUGUST By September, the potato blight has spread from southern Britain, Scotland, Belgium, and Holland to Ireland. 1846 - RELIEF EFFORTS BEGIN Workhouses are expanded, and government work projects begin. Three-fourths of the year’s potato crop is lost that fall. 1847 - MASS EVICTIONS BEGIN Soup kitchens feed over 3 million people a day. Landlords begin to evict tenant farmers and burn homes to avoid paying taxes. 1848 to 1849 - WORKHOUSES ARE FULL - DISEASE SPREADS Reports of cholera increase, especially in overcrowded, filthy workhouses. Two-thirds of the 1849 potato crop is lost. 1852 - BLIGHT GRADUALLY ENDS By 1852, the potato blight has ended. Over one million people have died, and another million have emigrated.
pages.brief: A wooden sailing ship crosses the Atlantic under a grey sky. Below deck, passengers lie packed tightly in dark, filthy bunks with too few blankets and little food or water. Sick, weak travellers huddle at the rail as the ship nears America.

pages.text: Aftermath The potato blight was over by 1852, but Ireland was changed forever. A million people had died, and over a million had emigrated. Many people who stayed in Ireland were homeless and jobless. The landlords could not make money, so they sold the land for other purposes or simply abandoned it rather than pay high taxes. With no land and no jobs, many Irish people continued to emigrate over the next decades. By 1861, the population of Ireland had dropped from over 8.5 million to 5 million; more than one in three people were gone. Ten years later, the population had dropped even further to 4.5 million. Many Irish people blamed Britain, the most powerful country in the world at that time, for not helping more. This bitterness would help fuel the revolution that finally split Ireland into two countries in 1922. The Two Irelands Since 1922, the island of Ireland has been divided into two countries. The independent Republic of Ireland is in the south. Northern Ireland is still part of the United Kingdom.
pages.brief: By 1852 the blight has passed but Ireland is changed. Homeless, jobless people walk past abandoned, overgrown fields and empty cottages. A small map shows the island divided into the independent Republic of Ireland in the south and Northern Ireland in the north.

pages.text: Conclusion Scientists eventually discovered that the potato plants died of a disease called late potato blight, which was caused by the funguslike organism Phytophthora infestans. Spores from the organism were blown by wind and washed into the soil by rain. Even after the Great Hunger, as the famine was called in Ireland, Irish immigration to the United States continued. Over five million people arrived between 1850 and 1920. Some ran for political office, and others started businesses. Famous Americans, including President John F. Kennedy and inventor Henry Ford, had ancestors who came to America during the famine. Today, forty million Americans proudly claim Irish roots, celebrate its folk traditions and holidays, and continue to popularize Irish literature, music, and film as an established part of world culture. The statue of Annie Moore and her brothers at Cobh Harbor, Ireland, has come to represent all of the famine emigrants who left Ireland in search of a better life.
pages.brief: Spores of the potato blight drift on the wind and wash into the soil with rain, seen landing on a potato leaf shown close up. At Cobh Harbour, a statue of young Annie Moore and her brothers stands on the quay, standing for all the emigrants who left.

pages.text: Oh, That’s Old! Imagine you’re in a dark, lovely forest. Trees with trunks wider than cars tower overhead and block almost all the sunlight. Small ferns and other plants soak up what little light they can find. Pine needles and other dead leaves cover the ground. Like something out of a fairy tale, an old- growth forest is a place of wonder and mystery.
pages.brief: A dark, lovely old-growth forest with trunks wider than cars towering overhead and blocking most sunlight. Small ferns and low plants soak up scant light. Pine needles and dead leaves carpet the forest floor. The scene feels mysterious and fairy-tale-like.

pages.text: Forest Levels Canopy Tall trees like Understory Small trees Forest floor Grasses, mosses, ferns, and logs Old-growth forests are some of the most beautiful and scientifically interesting places on Earth. Yet because of humans, many of them have shrunk or disappeared. By carefully studying and protecting the ones that remain, we can understand the complex and delicate ecosystems they create.
pages.brief: A layered old-growth forest shows tall canopy trees overhead, smaller understory trees below, and the forest floor with grasses, mosses, ferns, and fallen logs. The beautiful, scientifically interesting forest looks like a complex and delicate ecosystem.

pages.text: United States Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California together cover more than 1,353 square miles (3,504 sq km). They hold more than 300 square miles (777 sq km) of old-growth forest. This forest includes a variety of tree coniferous but deciduous as well. One of the of these is the giant sequoia. Found only in California, these huge trees are among the oldest on Earth. They can live for more than 3,000 years. A giant sequoia known as the General Sherman Tree is the largest tree in the world. The General Sherman Tree is the largest tree on the planet (but not the tallest).
pages.brief: In Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California, huge giant sequoia trees rise among coniferous and deciduous forest. One enormous sequoia, the General Sherman Tree, stands wide and tall, showing why it is the largest tree on the planet.

pages.text: Thousands of creatures live in the park, including the Pacific fisher. This relative of the weasel lives under the thick Fisher canopy in old-growth forests. It hunts birds and small mammals—but its favorite meal is porcupine. Because its habitat is limited to old-growth forests, it is now rare in California, Oregon, and Washington. Sequoia Redwood Sequoia vs. Redwood Giant redwoods and giant sequoias both grow in California. They have the same color bark. Both are huge, but they’re different. Giant redwoods are the tallest trees in the world. They can reach up to 378 feet (115 m)! Giant sequoias are the largest. At up to 40 feet (12 m) in diameter, they can grow almost twice as wide as redwoods. Redwoods grow best in fog. Sequoias need dry heat for their cones to open. Redwoods grow near sea level. Sequoias grow at 5,000 to 7,000 feet (1,524 to 2,134 m).
pages.brief: A Pacific fisher, a weasel relative, moves under the thick canopy of an old-growth forest, hunting birds and small mammals. A porcupine is nearby as its favorite meal. Giant sequoia and redwood trees show their huge trunks and bark.

pages.text: Autumn is colorful in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Across the United States in the Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee, Great Smoky Mountains National Park covers more than 800 square miles (2,072 sq km). Almost all of the park is forest, with old-growth forests only making up about 25 percent. Deciduous trees make up most of the old-growth forests in this area. Species include dogwood, Carolina silverbell, magnolia, American beech, yellow bird, and maple, among others.
pages.brief: Autumn colors fill Great Smoky Mountains National Park in the Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee. Deciduous old-growth trees, including dogwood, Carolina silverbell, magnolia, American beech, yellow bird, and maple, stand across the forested slopes.

pages.text: Northern flying squirrel The endangered Carolina northern flying squirrel makes its home among these trees. These small mammals don’t actually fly. They use skin attached at their front and back paws to glide. They mostly eat fungi and lichens but may also feed on fruits and nuts. Without the old-growth forest, these animals would vanish. Tough, Not Tall Not all old-growth forests feature towering trees. In some harsh places exposed to fierce and frigid winds, pines, spruces, and other coniferous trees become stunted and twisted. These trees are called Krummholz, a German word meaning “crooked wood.” They live near the Arctic and near timberline, the boundary on a mountain where the trees stop growing. They never grow much over 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, but don’t let their size fool you: Some are one thousand years old.
pages.brief: A small Carolina northern flying squirrel glides on skin stretched between its front and back paws among old-growth trees. Nearby, stunted, twisted coniferous Krummholz trees grow in a harsh, windy place near timberline, low but very old.

pages.text: A Seibold’s beech tree reaches for the sun in Shirakami-Sanchi, Japan. Japan In the northern part of Japan sits Shirakami- Sanchi. It’s one of the last untouched old-growth forests in East Asia. Made up mostly of Seibold’s beech trees, the area covers just 65 square miles (170 sq km) of the Shirakami Mountains. Forests like this one once covered most of northern Japan, but many have been cut down.
pages.brief: In Shirakami-Sanchi in northern Japan, a tall Seibold’s beech tree reaches toward the sun. The untouched old-growth forest covers the Shirakami Mountains, made up mostly of beech trees, though forests like it once spread across most of northern Japan.

pages.text: Almost completely untouched by humans, Shirakami-Sanchi has no trails or structures. Because of its steep slopes, no trees have been cut down. Wildlife within the area is protected, although hunters called Matagi are sometimes allowed to hunt bears as part of their religion. The forest is also home to the Japanese serow. This goatlike animal is only found here and in two other small areas in Japan. More than 2,100 insect species and 87 bird species live in the forests—including the black woodpecker, an endangered species in Japan. Japanese serow Black woodpeckers.
pages.brief: A steep, trail-less old-growth forest in Shirakami-Sanchi with no structures. A goatlike Japanese serow stands among the trees, and a black woodpecker clings to a trunk. Matagi hunters may sometimes hunt bears here as part of their religion.

pages.text: Fallen trees like this fir can nurse along other plants in this old-growth forest in the Caucasus region of Russia. Russia Russia’s Western Caucasus region stretches about 1,062 square miles (2,750 sq km) from the Black Sea to the Caucasus Mountains. Protected within Caucasus State Biosphere Reserve and Sochi National Park, this area shows great diversity. Coniferous trees make up most of the forests. Different species, such as pine, cedar, fir, and spruce—as well as beech and oak (both deciduous)—grow in different areas and at different elevations.
pages.brief: A fallen fir tree lies on the forest floor in the Western Caucasus region of Russia, nursing other plants as they grow. Coniferous trees, including pine, cedar, fir, and spruce, and deciduous beech and oak grow at different elevations from the Black Sea toward the Caucasus Mountains.

pages.text: Snow leopards A variety of endangered animals make their home in these forests. Some scientists think that a very small number of endangered snow leopards survive there. No sightings have been reported for years, but scientists still find signs of the large cats, such as paw prints and scat. The endangered wisent, or European bison, has also been returned to the forest. The last wild wisent was killed in the Western Caucasus in 1927. People set captive wisents free in the area in 1940. Wisents.
pages.brief: In the Western Caucasus forests, a rare snow leopard leaves paw prints and scat though no recent sightings are reported. An endangered wisent, or European bison, stands among the trees, returned after the last wild one was killed in 1927; people set captive wisents free there in 1940.

pages.text: The Future of Old-Growth Forests Old-growth forests often contain very complex ecosystems that have been supporting life for hundreds or even thousands of years. Governments, national parks, and organizations protect many of these places. However, other old-growth forests, both small and large, are in danger. Human actions ecosystems. Once gone, that these old- hold may be lost forever. Laws prevent logging in some old-growth forests but not others. People continue to debate how much protection is enough.
pages.brief: An old-growth forest shows a complex ecosystem that has supported life for hundreds or thousands of years. Some areas are protected by governments, parks, and organizations, while other old-growth forests face danger from human actions and debate over whether logging laws protect enough.

books.title: What Is Water Worth?
books.art_why: The book covers real places, people, water systems, and current environmental issues that can be photographed.

pages.text: Tadpoles race against time as their rock puddle shrinks.
pages.brief: Tadpoles swim and race in a small rock puddle as the water around them shrinks. The puddle is shallow, and the tadpoles are crowded together, struggling to stay in the remaining water. They have little room left as the puddle continues to dry.

pages.text: Russia’s Lake Baikal is the deepest and oldest freshwater lake in the world. It is also the largest by volume but not by surface area. Lake Superior holds that record. Water, Water Everywhere Many of us around the world take water for granted. Why shouldn’t we, when water is all around? It comes out of our faucets and collects in puddles on the sidewalk when it rains. Lakes and rivers brim with water. We buy water in bottles and slurp it from drinking fountains. In fact, if we had a drinking glass as big as the United States and filled it with every drop of water on the planet, the glass would have to be 145 kilometers (90 mi.) tall to hold it all. With so much water, you’d think everyone would have enough to drink. Not so!
pages.brief: Russia’s Lake Baikal lies in a vast landscape, deep and old. Lake Superior spreads wide across the surface. Elsewhere, water runs from a faucet, collects in a sidewalk puddle after rain, fills lakes and rivers, and pours from a drinking fountain. Bottles of water are ready to buy.

pages.text: Even though the region is water-starved, the people of Saudi Arabia can access water because it is a high-income country. Some countries have more fresh water than others, but most have enough water to meet people’s needs. What they don’t always have is the means to make that water available to people. High-income countries can tap into hard-to-get sources of water much more easily than low- income countries, where people often don’t have enough money to dig wells or build dams to create reservoirs. Today, we humans can only reach and use 1 percent of Earth’s freshwater. That 1 percent is under stress due to three underlying problems: pollution, increased demand driven by the world’s ever-growing population, and climate change.
pages.brief: In water-starved Saudi Arabia, people can access water because it is a high-income country. In a low-income country, people lack money to dig wells or build dams and reservoirs. Only 1 percent of Earth’s freshwater can be reached and used, and that small share is under stress.

pages.text: Many forms of waste pollute the Amazon River in Brazil. Pollution’s Impact Water pollution is a huge problem on many continents. South America’s Amazon rainforest spans 7 million square kilometers (2.7 million sq. mi.) and is home to about 30 million people and more than 30,000 plant species. For years, people have been dumping untreated human waste and toxic chemicals into the Amazon River. Drilling for oil and mining for gold have made some sections of the Amazon River toxic. In other low-income areas where fresh water often goes untreated, pollution makes people sick in other ways. Because people lack access to running water or indoor plumbing, human waste ends up outside.
pages.brief: The Amazon River flows through Brazil’s rainforest. Waste, untreated human waste, and toxic chemicals pollute its water. Drilling for oil and mining for gold make some sections toxic. In other low-income areas, people lack running water or indoor plumbing, so human waste ends up outside.

pages.text: Do You Know? Worldwide, more people have a mobile phone than a toilet. That waste, filled with bacteria, then flows into rivers and streams. People use the water in these toxic waterways for drinking, cooking, and bathing. According to the United Nations Development Program, half the world’s hospital beds contain patients sick from drinking unclean water. High-income countries such as the United States, where most people have access to clean drinking water, experience other challenges with pollution. The most common challenge comes from agriculture. Every time it rains, chemicals and animal waste from farming are washed into waterways. An aging system, oil, and other kinds of pollution all threaten U.S. waters as well. A Pennsylvania resident shows a jug of polluted water to an official in Washington, D.C., in 2014. He and other residents wanted fracking for oil and gas on nearby land to stop.
pages.brief: A Pennsylvania resident stands before an official in Washington, D.C., holding up a jug of polluted water. He and other residents want fracking for oil and gas on nearby land to stop. The scene shows people asking for action about polluted water.

pages.text: Population’s Impact In 2011, the human species hit a milestone. On October 30, a baby girl was born in the Philippines: the world’s 7 billionth person. By 2050, experts say that 9.7 billion people will be walking the planet, each looking for food, energy, land, and water. Growing populations reduce the amount of water available for each person. In 1950, the 2.5 billion people on Earth only used a third of the fresh water that we use today. Now, research shows that 1 in 9 people lack safe water to drink. Many live on less than 8 liters (2 gal.) a day. By 2050, more than half of the world’s people will be living in areas where water is scarce. High-income countries are far less likely to face polluted drinking water than low-income countries, but some face surging populations. This can lead to water shortages, in part because people in high-income countries use more water. Average Daily Water Use: Americans vs. Others 100 gallons (379 liters) 2 gallons (8 liters) Compare daily water use between Americans (left) and many low-income people around the world (above).
pages.brief: In the Philippines, a baby girl is born, marking the world’s seven billionth person. Around the world, a growing population looks for food, energy, land, and water. In one home, an American uses about 100 gallons a day; in another, a person in a low-income country uses about 2 gallons.

pages.text: In the United States, a four-person family, on average, uses 1,514 liters (400 gal.) of water a day, about 379 liters (100 gal.) per person. This level of use could last if only a few people were using the water. Instead, more and more people rely on limited water sources. For example, Los Angeles County’s population is expected to reach 13 million by 2050. Yet the area can only support 1 million people on its own water. Instead, Los Angeles—and many other cities in the western United States—pull their water from distant rivers. That river water is running out, owing to growing populations... and to climate change. Big Population = Big Water Demand.
pages.brief: A four-person family in the United States uses about 400 gallons of water a day. Los Angeles grows toward 13 million people, though the area can only support 1 million on its own water. The city pulls water from distant rivers that are running out.

pages.text: The Impact of Climate Change Climate change is already affecting people around the world by producing extreme weather conditions such as storms and floods. Yet the threat that climate change presents to the global water supply may be the worst threat of all. Scientists predict that by 2050, more than 5 billion people may face severe water shortages as a result of climate change. Climate change results from too much carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. These gases, produced in large part by the burning of fossil fuels, trap the Sun’s heat close to Earth’s surface, much like a greenhouse. The result is an overall increase in Earth’s temperature. That warming, in turn, leads to climate change. The warmer temperatures disrupt the water cycle, which is a delicate balance between evaporation and precipitation. Warmer temperatures increase the rate of surface water evaporation into the atmosphere. That, in turn, affects different parts of the world in different ways. Increased evaporation might dry out some areas while producing droughts in other areas. A drought is a long period of lower-than-normal precipitation that results in a shortage of water.
pages.brief: Storms and floods strike communities as climate change affects weather. Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases trap the Sun’s heat close to Earth, much like a greenhouse. Warmer temperatures disrupt the water cycle, increasing evaporation. Some areas dry out while others face drought.

pages.text: Regions at the highest risk of drought include the Mediterranean and the Middle East. In the United States, most scientists say that climate change is responsible for an extreme drought in the Southwest and California. The drought in the Southwest has been causing problems in the region since 1999. The water level of Lake Mead, on the border between Nevada and Arizona, has plummeted. The lake, which is fed by the Colorado River, is a source of fresh water for 25 million people. If rains don’t increase soon, odds are good that desert residents will have to start rationing water. A River Runs Dry Nearly 40 million people depend on the Colorado River. It now trickles to an end before it can reach the sea.
pages.brief: On the border between Nevada and Arizona, the water level of Lake Mead has dropped. The lake is fed by the Colorado River and is a source of fresh water for 25 million people. The Colorado River now trickles to an end before it can reach the sea.

pages.text: A boy fishes in the Daning River, one of many rivers fed by the Himalayas. Climate change is also responsible for the melting of glaciers high in the Himalaya mountains. The glaciers help provide fresh water for 1.5 billion people living in India, Pakistan, and six other Asian countries. In the past, the melting glaciers slowly released water into the rivers below. Now the glaciers are melting rapidly, and the long-term water supply is shrinking. At the same time, the increased melting has caused severe flooding along these rivers. As climate change worsens, less water is available for ranching, growing crops, and producing energy. Nature and wildlife suffer. Arguments break out between cities, states, and even countries over who has more right to the same source of water. For instance, Pakistan and India are in a race to build dams on the headwaters of the same river. Tensions between the two countries run high, and the growing water crisis hasn’t helped.
pages.brief: A boy fishes in the Daning River, one of many rivers fed by the Himalayas. High in the mountains, glaciers melt rapidly, causing severe flooding and shrinking the long-term water supply. Less water remains for ranching, crops, energy, and wildlife.

pages.text: Solving the Problem So what can we do? Each person’s efforts to conserve water can help. States can conserve, too. The Colorado River supplies water to much of the American West. While cities are growing rapidly, farming and ranching still use more than 70 percent of the river’s water. Should some of that water go to cities instead? Countries need to find solutions, too. Workers in Saudi Arabia are converting salt water to fresh water in a process called desalination. The process is expensive, though, and many countries cannot afford to build desalination plants.
