Spain is a country located in southwestern Europe on the Iberian Peninsula. It lies south of the Pyrenees (PEER-uh-neez) mountains and stretches all the way to the Strait of Gibraltar— a body of water that separates Spain from the continent of Africa. France borders Spain to the northeast, and Portugal borders it to the west. The Balearic Islands off Spain’s eastern coast form an archipelago in the Mediterranean Sea. It is a Spanish province known for its beautiful beaches and rich holiday traditions. The Canary Islands off the western coast of Morocco are a Spanish region and also a popular beach destination.
pages.brief: A map shows Spain on the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe, bordered by France and Portugal, with the Pyrenees, Strait of Gibraltar, Mediterranean Sea, Atlantic Ocean, Balearic Islands, Canary Islands, and nearby Morocco.

pages.text: Farmers grow more than two hundred types of olives in Spain. Spain overtook Italy in 2014 as the world’s largest producer of olive oil. People The population of Spain is estimated to be fewer than forty-eight million people. The urban population far exceeds that of the rural areas. About three-quarters of the population lives in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, and other smaller cities. Tourism employs about two million people and is very important to Spain’s economy. The auto industry remains one of Spain’s largest employers. Other industries include textiles, food, clothing, shipbuilding, and the making of medical equipment. On top of that, Spain proudly produces and exports more olive oil than any other country in the world.
pages.brief: Farmers tend olive trees in Spain, growing more than two hundred types of olives. The agricultural scene shows work that helps Spain produce and export more olive oil than any other country in the world.

pages.text: Spain is a member of the European Union (EU). The EU began in 1951 with the countries of Belgium, Germany, France, Luxembourg, and Italy as members. Its purpose was to have countries work together to solve common issues such as trade, security, and the rights of citizens. Most EU members share a currency called the euro. As of 2022, the EU had twenty-seven member nations. Spain’s official language is Spanish, or Castilian, and most people speak it. Depending on the region, people also speak Basque, Galician, and Catalan languages. Textile workers prepare clothing to be sold in stores (right). People enjoy a sidewalk cafe in Palma, Spain (below).
pages.brief: Textile workers prepare clothing to be sold in stores, while other people enjoy a sidewalk cafe in Palma, Spain. The page links Spain with the European Union, shared euro currency, and languages such as Spanish, Basque, Galician, and Catalan.

pages.text: Spain’s Landforms ATLANTIC OCEAN S E A E A N A N E R R I T E D M Land Spain’s varied landscape ranges from high plateaus in its interior to dry, desert-like regions in the south. Beautiful beaches and mountain ranges around the country create distinct environments. The Meseta Central, a plateau in central Spain, covers about half the country. People mine silver, lead, and copper and raise livestock in the mountains that border the Meseta. The dramatic and rocky Sierra Nevada mountain chain rises over southern Spain, with Mount Mulhacén (moo-lah-THEN) towering over the entire range. The Sierra Nevada is part of the Andalusian (an-duh-LOO-zhuhn) region in the southeast. The Pyrenees mountains lie to the north and form a solid natural border between Spain and France.
pages.brief: Spain’s varied landscape includes high plateaus in the interior and dry, desert-like regions in the south. The Meseta Central covers about half the country, while the rocky Sierra Nevada and Mount Mulhacén rise over southern Spain, and the Pyrenees form a natural border with France.

pages.text: The Pyrenees mountain chain stretches from the eastern shores of the Mediterranean Sea to the coastline of the Atlantic Ocean in the west. The chain extends for 434 kilometers (270 mi.). The western part of the mountain range is a lush, rolling, heavily wooded countryside. In the east, vineyards and orchards are plentiful. The central region includes a rich display of granite peaks, deep canyons, waterfalls, and hundreds of mountain lakes. Several groups of people—the Andorran, Catalan, Béarnese (bair-NEEZ), and Basque—call the Pyrenees mountains their home. Traditionally, they make a living through agriculture and raising livestock. A wide variety of animals also live in these mountains. The brown bear, a species of goat- antelope called the chamois (sham-WAH), and the rare bearded vulture all live in the Pyrenees. Forests of fir, pine, and oak cover the slopes of the Pyrenees mountains.
pages.brief: The Pyrenees stretch from the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean, with wooded slopes, vineyards, orchards, granite peaks, canyons, waterfalls, and mountain lakes. Andorran, Catalan, Béarnese, and Basque people live there, raising livestock and farming, while brown bears, chamois, and bearded vultures inhabit forests of fir, pine, and oak.

pages.text: Moors built the Alhambra, a palace and fortress, in Granada, Spain, on a high point overlooking the entire valley. History People from Phoenicia (fi-NEE-shuh) settled southern Spain around 800 bce. Phoenicia is Lebanon, Syria, and Israel today. Phoenicians were skilled artisans and sailors who traded ivory and perfumes for bronze and silver goods. Greek traders from Carthage (now Tunisia) followed around 500 bce and brought with them olive trees and grapes. Then, around 200 bce, the Romans arrived and ruled Spain for about six hundred years. They made roads and bridges that connected towns. They also built aqueducts that carried water from rivers to cities. Germanic people came from the north after the Romans. Then, Muslim settlers known as Moors arrived in 711 ce and ruled until the Catholic era. Moorish buildings can still be seen in Spain today, including monuments such as the Alhambra, a palace in Granada built in the 1300s, and the Great Mosque of Córdoba.
pages.brief: People from Phoenicia settle southern Spain around 800 BCE, followed by Greek traders, Romans, Germanic people, and Muslim Moors in 711 CE. Moorish buildings remain today, including the Alhambra, a palace and fortress in Granada built on a high point overlooking the valley, and the Great Mosque of Córdoba.

pages.text: For many centuries, Spain had been divided into kingdoms. The main ones were Aragon, Castile, and Granada. Two of these kingdoms became one when King Ferdinand II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile married. They were Catholic monarchs who won a war against the Moors for control of Granada. The king and queen set up the Spanish Inquisition, a group that killed people who were not Catholic. The Inquisition also pushed Jewish and Muslim people out of Spain. Ferdinand and Isabella paid explorers such as Christopher Columbus to find new trade routes for Spain to Asia. When Columbus arrived in the New World (islands in the Caribbean Sea), Spain set up colonies there. They brought gold, silver, spices, and enslaved people back to Europe. At the time, much of Spain’s wealth was built on the slave trade with Africa and the Americas. During the 1800s and early 1900s, inequality between the rich and the poor led people to try overthrowing the elected government. When that failed, the Spanish Civil War broke out in 1936 and lasted until 1939. When the war ended, General Francisco Franco took control of the country and ruled as a dictator until his death in 1975. After Franco’s death, King Juan Carlos I became the next king. He then made Adolfo Suárez—who brought democracy to Spain—prime minister.
pages.brief: King Ferdinand II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile marry and become Catholic monarchs, winning control of Granada and setting up the Spanish Inquisition. They pay Christopher Columbus to find trade routes, while later inequality leads to the Spanish Civil War, Franco’s dictatorship, and King Juan Carlos I’s move toward democracy.

pages.text: Celebrations Spanish people look forward to local holidays called fiestas, or festivals. These holidays often celebrate local harvests, historical events, or saints. Lively and fun, they include dancing, singing, parades, and fireworks. St. George’s Day, on April 23, is a time for people to give loved ones books and red roses. In July, Pamplona hosts the Festival of San Fermín. During this festival, people try to dodge bulls as they run through the streets of Pamplona. National Day takes place on October 12. This is the date that Spain first arrived in the Americas. For Spanish people, it is also the date that honors Spain as an important country in the world. La Tomatina La Tomatina is a yearly festival held in honor of a patron saint. It is likely the world’s biggest tomato fight. At this festival, ripened tomatoes are brought in by the truckload, and people throw tomatoes at one another—just for fun.
pages.brief: Spanish people celebrate local fiestas with dancing, singing, parades, and fireworks. On St. George’s Day they give books and red roses; in Pamplona people run through the streets dodging bulls during the Festival of San Fermín; and at La Tomatina, trucks bring ripened tomatoes for a huge tomato fight.

pages.text: Tapas Tapas are finger foods that can be eaten cold or hot and are usually served on small plates. People serve shrimp and squid along the Spanish coasts, while people serve sausages inland. Food Spanish people usually eat three meals a day. A Spanish breakfast might be coffee, milk, or hot chocolate, a sweet roll, and sometimes cereal. They eat lunch—the biggest meal of the day—around two in the afternoon. Lunch may include soup, salad, a main course, and dessert. Dinner is a lighter meal. It is served late, anywhere from nine to eleven in the evening. Each region in Spain enjoys its own style of food. Regions near the ocean typically serve seafood. People in central Spain often eat beans, lentils, lamb, and pork. Valencia, known for its rice dishes, is famous for paella—a rice dish that can be made with fish, meat, and vegetables. A delicious and popular soup called gazpacho comes from the Andalusian region of Spain. Made with tomatoes and other vegetables, the soup is often served cold in the summer as a refreshing meal.
pages.brief: Tapas are finger foods served on small plates, with shrimp and squid along the coasts and sausages inland. Spanish people eat three meals a day, lunch being the biggest around two in the afternoon; Valencia is famous for paella, and the Andalusian region serves cold gazpacho made with tomatoes and vegetables in summer.

pages.text: Antoni Gaudí which stands in Barcelona, Spain. Construction began in 1882 and it still continues. Conclusion Many Spanish people are proud of their culture. Although many identify with the town or region they’re from, their celebrations and festivals bring them together as a nation. Some regions still try to preserve their own traditions, but the country has been unified for many years. Spain is one of the most lively cultural centers in the European Union. It boasts an amazing heritage due in part to the arrival of people from many different parts of the world who have brought celebrations, food, and architecture to Spanish culture. Spain’s history is long and complex, and its culture and past actions have impacted many parts of the world. Spain’s beauty and the warmth of its people help make our world a more interesting place to live in.
pages.brief: A building designed by Antoni Gaudí stands in Barcelona, Spain. Construction began in 1882 and still continues. Spanish people are proud of their culture, and celebrations and festivals bring them together as a nation, while regions preserve traditions and architecture from many parts of the world.

pages.text: The Fraidy-Cat of Empress of Ireland Emmy was considered the ship’s cat on the Empress of Ireland. The day before the ship sailed from Canada, Emmy fled the vessel two times. Her behavior was viewed as a bad sign. The next day, the Empress of Ireland struck another ship and sank in just fourteen minutes. More than one thousand people died, making it the deadliest wreck in Canadian history. Ghost Ship: Mary Celeste Some lost ships experience a fate even more mysterious than sinking to the bottom of the sea. On November 7, 1872, the cargo ship Mary Celeste set sail from New York, Mary Celeste bound for Italy. The 30.1-meter (100 ft.) vessel had a crew of seven, plus the captain and his family. One month later, a British ship spotted a vessel drifting in the Atlantic Ocean. It was the Mary Celeste, but a boarding party found no one on the ship. The navigational equipment and a lifeboat were missing, but there were no signs of violence. All cargo and gear were left behind. The last entry in the captain’s log held no clues about a possible problem. The captain, his family, and the crew were never seen again. The lack of answers has led to many imagined accounts of the mystery. They usually feature treachery, murder, and even sea monsters.
pages.brief: Emmy, the ship's cat on the Empress of Ireland, flees the vessel twice before it sails. The next day, the passenger ship strikes another ship and sinks in fourteen minutes. In another scene, the Mary Celeste drifts empty in the Atlantic, with cargo and gear left behind and no one from the captain, family, or crew ever seen again.

pages.text: A painting of HMS Erebus stuck in the ice by François Etienne Musin The Long Hunt for HMS Erebus and HMS Terror In 1845, the British navy mounted the Franklin Expedition to search for a shortcut for shipping between Europe and Asia. The expedition included 129 people on two ships—HMS Terror and HMS Erebus. On July 26, 1845, two whaling ships spotted Terror and Erebus in Canada’s Baffin Bay. Then two years passed with no word from the expedition’s commander. Officials and the public feared for the safety of the explorers.
pages.brief: HMS Erebus and HMS Terror, two British navy ships on the Franklin Expedition, are seen in Canada's Baffin Bay as two whaling ships spot them in July 1845. The ships are surrounded by ice. Officials and the public wait anxiously for word from the expedition commander, but two years pass with no news.

pages.text: Search and rescue ships eventually discovered abandoned gear, graves, and notes left behind by desperate crew members on uninhabited islands. The two ships had been trapped in pack ice in September 1846, and the commander of the expedition died the following June. For two years, the sailors—sick and dying—waited for the ice to release their ships. Finally, in April 1848, the survivors attempted a desperate hike southward to reach the Canadian mainland. In 1855, local Inuit told investigators about a group of Europeans who had starved to death along the coast. Evidence showed that the group had resorted to cannibalism to try to survive. In 2014, a ship equipped with sonar found the wreck of the Erebus. It was well preserved in 12 meters (40 ft.) of Arctic waters. Its partner ship, also well preserved, was found in September 2016 about 72 kilometers (45 mi.) away. A diver explores the remains of the Erebus.
pages.brief: On uninhabited Arctic islands, search parties find abandoned gear, graves, and notes left by desperate crew members. The survivors later attempt a hike southward toward the Canadian mainland. In a modern underwater scene, a diver explores the well-preserved wreck of HMS Erebus in Arctic water, located with sonar.

pages.text: Terror on the Rocks: SS Valencia The SS Valencia was one of the most terrifying shipwrecks of all. In January 1906, the passenger steamer was on its way to Seattle with 173 people on board. Near midnight on January 22, its iron hull ran aground near Vancouver Island. Pounding waves trapped the ship. The crew lowered lifeboats, but most boats flipped, or capsized, in the churning seas. People were tossed into freezing water, where they drowned. High winds and waves hampered rescue efforts. About thirty-six hours after the stranding, witnesses onshore watched in horror as a huge wave swept over the upper deck, where dozens of passengers were holding on for their lives. In total, only 37 out of 136 passengers survived. A Valencia lifeboat escapes the violent seas. It bears some of the few survivors of the wreck.
pages.brief: The SS Valencia, a passenger steamer, runs aground near Vancouver Island at night. Pounding waves trap the ship as the crew lower lifeboats that capsize in churning seas. People are tossed into freezing water. About thirty-six hours later, a huge wave sweeps over the upper deck where dozens of passengers hold on, while a lifeboat carries survivors away.

pages.text: Valencia leaves San Francisco eight years before the ship’s tragic sinking. How, why, and where were not the mysteries of the Valencia wreck. Investigations concluded that the captain and crew had made bad decisions that endangered the ship and its passengers. Most of the mysteries came later and inspired supernatural tales. In 1910, for example, newspapers reported that sailors had seen a ghostly Valencia sailing near the site of the wreck. A rumor also spread that a lifeboat filled with skeletons had been found in a nearby cave, though the story was never confirmed. Then in 1933—twenty-seven years after the disaster—one of Valencia ’s lifeboats was discovered in a nearby bay. Its nameplate is now displayed in the Maritime Museum of British Columbia.
pages.brief: The SS Valencia is shown leaving San Francisco eight years before its sinking. Later, sailors report seeing a ghostly Valencia near the wreck site. In a nearby cave, an unconfirmed rumor tells of a lifeboat filled with skeletons. In 1933, one of Valencia's lifeboats is discovered in a nearby bay, and a museum display preserves a piece from it.

pages.text: The disappearance of USS Cyclops, pictured above, remains the largest loss of life in U.S. naval history in an event not directly related to combat. Gone Without a Trace: USS Cyclops USS Cyclops was a huge U.S. Navy supply ship. While serving during World War I, the Cyclops crew picked up a heavy load of ore in Brazil. While there, Captain W. Worley reported to his superiors that one of the engines needed repairs and was not operational. He was told to get it fixed once he reached the United States. On February 22, 1918, the ship left Brazil for Baltimore with 309 crew members. Cyclops disappeared somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean. Not a single piece of wreckage has ever been found. At the time, people wondered if a German submarine had sunk the ship. Some naval officials wondered if Captain Worley, who had been born in Germany, might have secretly handed the ship over to the enemy, though there was no proof of that.
pages.brief: USS Cyclops, a huge U.S. Navy supply ship, takes on a heavy load of ore in Brazil during World War I. Captain W. Worley reports one engine is not operational. On February 22, 1918, the ship leaves Brazil for Baltimore with 309 crew members, then disappears in the Atlantic. No wreckage is found, and people wonder about a German submarine.

Another theory notes that the ship disappeared in the Bermuda Triangle. This area in the Atlantic Ocean has a reputation for swallowing ships. pages.text: There and Gone: SS Edmund Fitzgerald On November 9, 1975, SS Edmund Fitzgerald, a huge freighter, left Superior, Wisconsin, fully loaded with iron ore. A storm was forecast, but the captain was not concerned. On the afternoon of November 10, the U.S. Coast Guard warned all ships to seek shelter. The Edmund Fitzgerald headed for Whitefish Bay, Wisconsin. At about 7:00 p.m., the captain reported the ship was taking on water but radioed, “We are holding our own.” Moments later, the ship no longer appeared on radar. No lifeboats were launched. None of the twenty- nine crew members were found. Days later, the Coast Guard located the wreck on the lake floor. The ship had been snapped in half. Investigators suspect a series of three rogue waves may have sunk the ship so quickly that there was no time even to make a distress call. Rogue Waves Researchers suspect “rogue waves” for some unexplained shipping disasters. What makes these waves so dangerous is their unpredictability, size, and power. A rogue wave comes out of nowhere and is much bigger than the waves around it. It is created by a powerful combination of strong water currents and high winds, usually far out at sea. The sudden jump in wave size can flip large freighters.
pages.brief: SS Edmund Fitzgerald, a huge freighter loaded with iron ore, sails on Lake Superior as a storm gathers. The captain radios that the ship is taking on water. Later, the broken wreck lies on the lake floor. In a separate scene, a towering rogue wave rises far out at sea, created by strong currents and high winds.

pages.text: The Slave Wrecks Project Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, as many as one thousand ships carrying enslaved people were lost at sea. Most of those shipwrecks remain undiscovered and undocumented today. Organizations such as the Slave Wrecks Project, founded in 2008, are working to find those lost ships and the historical information they contain. In 2014, the Slave Wrecks Project made its first major recovery. It found a sunken ship near the coast of Cape Town, South Africa. The Sea Keeps Many Secrets Sailing the seas has always involved an element of danger. The oceans stretch vast distances, and the weather can suddenly turn foul. Also, reefs and rocks often hide along coastlines. Modern equipment makes shipping safer than ever. Even so, dozens of shipwrecks still claim the lives of about two thousand people every year. Working on a ship remains one of the world’s most dangerous jobs. Sailors entrust their lives to their knowledge, skills, and the ships they serve on. Still, sometimes, their fate is a matter of luck. Every shipwreck leaves behind mysteries. Some of these mysteries can be explored and eventually explained, and older wrecks may provide us with a glimpse into the past. Much of the time, though, the sea’s secrets are never revealed.
pages.brief: Underwater archaeologists from the Slave Wrecks Project examine a sunken ship carrying enslaved people near Cape Town, South Africa. Above, a modern ship sails a vast, dangerous ocean with sudden foul weather and hidden reefs along the coast. The scene suggests the many shipwrecks that still claim lives every year and the secrets the sea keeps.

books.title: 1849: The California Gold Rush
books.art_why: The book covers a historical event from 1848–1852 whose key moments and routes are best shown with period-style drawings.

pages.text: Prospectors mine in California around 1852.
pages.brief: Prospectors are shown mining in California around 1852. The miners are at work at a gold-mining site, focused on their tasks. The scene presents the prospectors and their mining work in the setting shown, without adding other places or events.

pages.text: Keeping a Secret On the morning of January 24, 1848, James Marshall went to inspect the ditch that carried water from the American River through the new sawmill his crew was building in California. The crew had deepened the section of the ditch that ran out of the mill to make the water flow more quickly. At the end of the ditch, about six inches under the water, he spotted something shiny. Marshall collected several pieces and showed his crew. They tested the pieces. It was gold! Marshall showed the gold to the owner of the mill, John Sutter, who controlled forty-eight thousand acres of land in California he called “New Switzerland” after his home country. Sutter bought the land from the Mexican government, but it actually belonged to the Indigenous Nisenan people. Sutter had taken more than land. Sutter’s deal with the Mexican government required that he not harm any of the Nisenan people in the area. Nevertheless, he trained many Native people to become part of his own private army and kidnapped and enslaved other Native people to work the land. Sutter tried to get everyone to keep the secret that gold had been discovered. He wanted to keep the riches for himself.
pages.brief: James Marshall stands at the mill ditch on the American River on January 24, 1848, inspecting the water. He has collected shiny pieces of gold and shows them to his crew; John Sutter is nearby, wanting the discovery kept secret.

pages.text: Panning Unlike gold in most places, California’s gold wasn’t locked deep under the ground. Erosion had long ago washed the metal down the mountains and into rivers. Miners used a technique called placer mining that allowed them to sift gold out of the riverbed using a shallow, flat pan. Placer because gold is much heavier than gravel. Prospectors stood in rivers and shoveled gravel into their pan. They removed large rocks, then carefully swirled the pan. The dirt and gravel spilled over the edges with the water. The shiny flakes of gold Each day, most miners only found gold stayed at the bottom that would be worth between $10 and $15 today. of the pan. Word Wise The term prospector means a person who moves to a spot with the prospect, or possibility, of finding gold and becoming rich.
pages.brief: Prospectors stand in a California river, shoveling gravel into shallow, flat pans. They remove large rocks and carefully swirl the pans so water spills dirt and gravel over the edges, leaving shiny flakes of gold at the bottom.

pages.text: The Forty-Niners Rumors soon swirled in the eastern states about gold out West. A California official sent a report about the gold to Washington, D.C.—along with a sample. In December 1848, the president told Congress A gold miner shovels gravel about the discovery. It was true! in California in 1852. Gold fever—the greed and contagious excitement brought on by the discovery of gold— took hold of many people. At the time, many workers earned less than a dollar a day. For them, it was the opportunity of a lifetime. In 1849, around ninety thousand people—called forty-niners — joined the Gold Rush. Around 10 percent, or nine thousand, were women. The forty-niners came from across the United States as well as from Mexico, Central and South America, Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. Black people were among the forty-niners as well. Around 200 to 300 were enslaved and had been forced by their enslavers to go to California. Free Black people also traveled west in hopes of finding gold. By 1852, around 2,000 Black people lived in California, which was about 1 percent of the population.
pages.brief: A gold miner shovels gravel in California in 1852. He works at a gold-mining site, bent to the task. The scene shows the miner’s labor during the Gold Rush era, with no other people or places added.

pages.text: The trip to the gold mines could take months—and was not cheap. People had to pay for transportation and supplies to last until they arrived in California. Many forty-niners left behind jobs and families. They planned to make a fortune quickly and return home. Others were ready for whatever adventure they found. People from California, Oregon, and Mexico were the first to show up at the rivers near Sutter’s Mill. pages.brief: People from California, Oregon, and Mexico arrive first at rivers near Sutter’s Mill with pack animals. Other forty-niners take long, costly journeys, some crossing Panama and others traveling by boat from the East; the scene shows these different routes toward California.

pages.text: By Ship About half of the forty-niners decided to travel by ship to avoid crossing the lands of Native peoples. It took ships between five and eight months to sail from the East Coast, around the tip of South America, and back up to California. The cheapest ticket was $75—about $2,300 in today’s money. Lodging was a tiny bunk in the bottom of the ship. Passengers ate dried meat and hard biscuits filled with weevils, and drank water. They suffered as a result of shipwrecks, seasickness, and disease. Many reported that Posters like this one advertised ships the worst things were that would carry forty-niners from crowding and boredom. New York City to San Francisco. Some passengers decided to save time by taking a shortcut through Panama. They could canoe and hike across 60 miles (97 km) of jungle, then catch another ship. These forty-niners faced an extreme environment with hazards they were unfamiliar with, including bad weather and wild animals. Many fell ill. If they made it across, there was still a risk that they would have to wait weeks or months to catch a ship on the other side.
pages.brief: Forty-niners crowd aboard a ship sailing from the East Coast around South America toward California. Passengers endure tiny bunks, dried meat, hard biscuits, water, seasickness, crowding, and boredom. Some travelers take the Panama shortcut, canoeing and hiking through jungle hazards.

pages.text: A drawing from around 1900 shows people traveling together in a group of wagons called a train. By Wagon It took about the same amount of time to get to California by wagon. Much of the land between forty-niners on the East Coast and California still belonged to Native peoples. Settlers moving out West often hunted without permission, stole from Native peoples, and attacked them. Native peoples thus viewed them with hostility. Most people left from Saint Louis, Missouri, the westernmost U.S. city at the time. Wagons followed the California Trail for 2,100 miles (3,380 km) across the flat prairie. A wagon could travel about 15 miles (24 km) in a day—if it didn’t break down, there wasn’t much rain, and the oxen stayed healthy. The forty-niners had to get the wagons across rivers, up mountains, down cliffs, and across deserts.
pages.brief: A wagon train of forty-niners travels together across the flat prairie on the California Trail. The wagons move about fifteen miles in a day when they do not break down, rain is light, and the oxen stay healthy. They must cross rivers, mountains, cliffs, and deserts.

pages.text: They were pounded by rain, wind, and snow. In addition to bad weather, other dangers facing forty-niners came from disease, starvation, and accidents. For those who made it to California, life did not get easier. Prospectors lived in mining camps made of tents and rough shelters, and worked twelve hours a day. Many fell ill, often due to poor conditions and diet. Despite these challenges, it was difficult to give up—the next pan of gravel might be worth a fortune! Gold miners stand in their camp at El Dorado, California, around 1850. The original El Dorado in South America is a mythical place of immense wealth.
pages.brief: Gold miners stand in their mining camp at El Dorado, California, around 1850. The camp is made of tents and rough shelters. The miners face rain, wind, snow, disease, starvation, accidents, and twelve-hour workdays while hoping the next pan brings fortune.

pages.text: Equal Opportunity? For Native peoples, the Gold Rush was disastrous. It opened the gateway to the West. Throngs of adventurers and settlers poured into Native lands. Many different groups of Native peoples lived in California. As forty-niners moved out West, violent attacks forced Native peoples off much of their land. Thousands were killed, and thousands more died of disease. Once California became a state in 1850, the U.S. government took control of the land, including areas with gold. Soon, fear and hatred led to the killing of thousands of Native peoples. New laws allowed settlers to arrest Native people for minor wrongdoings. The government then forced them to pay their fines by working on ranches. Around three hundred thousand Native peoples lived in California before the Gold Rush. More than one hundred thousand were dead only twenty years later. Good Prospects, Bad Endings Several of the men involved in the original discovery of gold ended up with nothing to show for it. John Sutter lost his golden property when the United States would not recognize his land grant from Mexico. Sutter, along with Sam Brannan and James Marshall, eventually lost their fortunes.
pages.brief: Native peoples are forced off their land as forty-niners and settlers move west. Thousands are killed or die of disease; new laws allow their arrest and forced labor. John Sutter, Sam Brannan, and James Marshall eventually lose their fortunes.

pages.text: As the hills filled white miners began to oppose other for gold, especially Chinese miners. White prospectors forced miners from Chinese miners search for gold in California around 1850. outside the United States to leave the mines. Almost three thousand Chinese people came to California in 1851. A terrible crop season in China made that number rise to more than twenty thousand the next year. California taxed miners from outside the United States to prospect. Some U.S. miners wanted to make it so difficult for them to mine that they would leave. One in every five miners who came to California in 1849 died within six months. Even those who found gold often lost it to robbers, gambling, or paying high prices for everyday goods. Some early prospectors were successful. Most of the riches from gold went to large companies. They were able to mine with high-pressure jets of water or dig deep mines.
pages.brief: Chinese miners search for gold in California around 1850. White prospectors increasingly oppose miners from outside the United States, forcing them to leave the mines and taxing them. Most riches go to large companies using high-pressure water jets or deep mines.

Sam Brannan became one of the first millionaires in the United States. Levi Strauss sold pants tough enough to handle the work—blue jeans. Women, especially, had many more opportunities in the West. They started businesses cooking, running boarding houses, and washing clothes for the prospectors. pages.brief: Mary Ellen Pleasant, a Black American businesswoman connected to the Underground Railroad, is shown during the Gold Rush. Entrepreneurs like Sam Brannan and Levi Strauss profit by selling to miners. Women find opportunities running businesses, boarding houses, cooking, and washing clothes for prospectors.

pages.text: San Francisco in 1851 (top) and today (bottom) The Golden State The biggest winners of the Gold Rush were white settlers, the U.S. government, and wealthy investors. The Gold Rush was devastating to Native peoples, however. Around three hundred thousand settlers, mostly white, swarmed California. In the 1860s, the country began to connect the East and West by building the transcontinental railway, causing further destruction to Native lands. The Gold Rush changed the western United States forever. Today, California has more people than any other state. It has a huge economy —larger than that of most countries. Nearly two centuries after the Gold Rush, California still lives up to its nickname: the Golden State.
pages.brief: San Francisco is shown in 1851 and today, comparing the Gold Rush settlement with the modern city. Around three hundred thousand settlers, mostly white, swarmed California. The Gold Rush benefited white settlers, the U.S. government, and wealthy investors while devastating Native peoples and changing the western United States forever.

pages.text: Amsterdam was surrounded by a moat from 1480 to 1585. Its population surged in the 1600s as the city grew. Workers drained swamps and built three more canals around the downtown area. The four waterways were used for transportation, defense, and water management. Besides the main canals, Amsterdam has 161 others, totaling over 100 kilometers (62 mi.) in length, that divide the city into close to 100 small islands joined by over 1,200 bridges. Although the canals were the city’s main transportation routes for centuries, they are now mainly used by smaller boats. However, they are still an important part of the city’s character. Reine, Norway A tiny Norwegian fishing village more than 100 kilometers (62 mi.) above the Arctic Circle has earned the nickname “The Most Beautiful Place in the World.” Located along the coast of one of the Lofoten Islands, Reine offers fishing, kayaking, skiing, whale watching, hiking, and gorgeous beaches. It’s also a perfect place for dramatic views of the northern lights.
pages.brief: In Amsterdam, canals surround the downtown area, with small boats traveling the waterways and many bridges linking close to one hundred islands; farther north, Reine, a tiny Norwegian fishing village on a Lofoten Island, sits by the sea beneath dramatic northern lights.

pages.text: ASIA Singapore Singapore is one of the world’s busiest port cities. Asia Singapore Singapore is the world’s only island city-state— an island that is both a city and an independent country. It is made up of sixty-three islands. Singapore depends on goods from other places since it has few natural resources of its own. The country must import almost everything it needs. Singapore’s land area has increased by almost 25 percent since the 1960s. Unlike Amsterdam, which has reclaimed land by removing seawater, Singapore has added land by dumping rocks and sand into the water. A project begun in 2016 will use Amsterdam’s methods to increase its land area.
pages.brief: Singapore, a busy port city and island city-state, is one of sixty-three islands, with ships and goods arriving from other places; workers dump rocks and sand into the water to add land and expand the city’s land area.

pages.text: Dubai, United Arab Emirates Dubai is a modern city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The city is the site of many construction projects. One of Dubai’s largest construction projects is Palm Islands—three artificial islands shaped like palm trees. The islands are being built along the coast by piling up huge amounts of sand and rock. They are adding hundreds of miles of coastline to the city as well as homes for many thousands of people. Construction began in 2001, and the first one was completed in late 2016. A curved seawall around the island protects it from ASIA strong waves and storms. Dubai INDIAN OCEAN Palm Jumeirah is one of the largest artificial islands in the world.
pages.brief: Dubai’s Palm Jumeirah, one of the world’s largest artificial islands, is shaped like a palm tree along the coast; workers pile up huge amounts of sand and rock to build three artificial islands, while a curved seawall protects the new land from strong waves and storms.

pages.text: The village of Ganvié is sometimes called Ganvié the Venice of Africa. AFRICA Africa Ganvié, Benin In startling contrast to the modern cities of Singapore and Dubai is Ganvié (GAWN-vye), the largest stilt village in Africa. The village is located in Lake Nokoué (NOHK-we) in the country of Benin. Ganvié has about twenty thousand residents and three thousand buildings. Only the school and a cemetery are located on land. Ganvié began during the seventeenth century, at a time when humans in West Africa were being captured and sold as slaves by Europeans. During that period, a powerful tribe called the Fon also captured and sold people from other tribes into slavery. The Fons’ religion forbade them from pursuing people who lived on water. Another tribe, the Tofinu, escaped to Lake Nokoué to avoid capture. They founded the stilt village and set up a way of life that continues to this day. Their success is reflected in the name of their village, which means “we survived.”
pages.brief: Ganvié, a large stilt village in Lake Nokoué in Benin, shows about twenty thousand residents living in three thousand buildings raised over the water; only the school and a cemetery stand on land, while long canoes move between the stilts.

pages.text: Villagers mainly make their living by fishing. They keep and breed fish using underwater fences. They also keep chickens and goats on patches of grass that grow in the water. People travel in long, narrow canoes called pirogues. Fadiouth (Shell Island), Senegal The residents of Fadiouth (fad-YOOT), Senegal, live on an island made up entirely of clamshells. For over three centuries, they have been eating clams and recycling the shells to make not only buildings and streets but also the land itself. The shells are held in place by the roots of trees and reeds.
pages.brief: In Ganvié, villagers fish from long, narrow pirogues and keep chickens and goats on patches of grass in the water; in Fadiouth, Senegal, residents live on an island made entirely of clamshells, with buildings and streets built from recycled shells held by tree roots and reeds.

pages.text: Uros SOUTH AMERICA The Uru people make reed canoes for transportation. South America Uros Floating Village, Peru Like the people of Ganvié Lake Village, the residents of Uros, a floating village in Peru, moved to water for safety. The Uru people escaped to Lake Titicaca over five hundred years ago. At that time, the Inca and Colla peoples took over their land. Approximately two thousand Uru now live on about seventy floating islands made of reeds. The islands, which are 1.2 to 2.4 meters (4–8 ft.) thick, break down from the bottom. New reeds must always be added on top. The Uru people also use the reeds to make canoes, homes, and furniture. They make their living from fishing and selling crafts. Even though the Uru live by traditional ways, they have some modern conveniences. Uros has its own radio station, and some residents have solar panels and motorboats.
pages.brief: The Uru people of Uros, a floating village on Lake Titicaca in Peru, live on about seventy reed islands; they make reed canoes, homes, and furniture, fish, and sell crafts, and some residents have solar panels, motorboats, and their own radio station.

pages.text: NORTH AMERICA Mexcaltitán Mexcaltitán sits on a 400-meter (1,300 ft.) sandbar off Mexico’s coast. North America Mexcaltitán, Mexico The Aztec people ruled large areas of Mesoamerica between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. According to legend, they came from a mythical island in a lagoon, and their gods told them to seek out a new homeland. After searching for two hundred years, they founded Tenochtitlán, their capital city. After the Spanish conquest in 1521, Tenochtitlán became known as Mexico City.
pages.brief: Mexcaltitán sits on a four-hundred-meter sandbar off Mexico’s coast; according to Aztec legend, the people came from a mythical island in a lagoon, searched for two hundred years, then founded Tenochtitlán, their capital city, which became Mexico City after the Spanish conquest.

pages.text: Mexcaltitán (mes-kahl-tee-TAHN) is a small human-made island near the Pacific coast of Mexico. Some historians think Aztec civilization began there. Records show that the early Aztecs used small canoes like those used by Mexcaltitán’s residents. In addition, a map from 1579 shows the mythical island and Mexcaltitán to be in the same place. Mexcaltitán, which is about 350 meters (1,150 ft.) by 40 meters (130 ft.), is now home to about eight hundred people. They live in houses made of adobe, brick, and cement. Many make their living by catching shrimp for local restaurants. This water town is sometimes called the Mexican Venice. In summer, during the rainy season, boats are the only way to travel through the streets. Children have fun playing “water soccer” on the island’s only soccer field, which is underwater. Locals boat and swim in the streets during the flood season in Mexcaltitán.
pages.brief: Mexcaltitán, a small human-made island near Mexico’s Pacific coast, has about eight hundred people in adobe, brick, and cement houses; in the rainy season, boats are the only way through the flooded streets, children play water soccer on the underwater soccer field, and locals boat and swim.

pages.text: Auckland is New Zealand’s largest city. AUSTRALIA Auckland Oceania Auckland, New Zealand This modern city of 1.5 million people is on the North Island of New Zealand in the South Pacific Ocean. Auckland is located between two large harbors on an isthmus less than 2 kilometers (1.2 mi.) wide at its narrowest point. The harbors open to the Pacific Ocean to the east and the Tasman Sea to the west. Auckland’s nickname is the “City of Sails.” About one-sixth of Aucklanders own a boat, and the city has hosted the America’s Cup yacht race twice. The city has thousands of beaches. Water- related activities include kayaking, parasailing, swimming, surfing, fishing, diving, and beach horseback riding.
pages.brief: Auckland, New Zealand’s largest city, lies on the North Island between two large harbors on a narrow isthmus; about one-sixth of Aucklanders own a boat, and people enjoy kayaking, parasailing, swimming, surfing, fishing, diving, and beach horseback riding along thousands of beaches.

pages.text: California Italy Aircraft carrier People and Water Many kinds of water cities exist besides the ones you’ve just read about. For instance, Italy has a tiny fishing town made up of brightly colored homes built on steep, rocky cliffs. Northern California has a floating community made up of different kinds of houseboats. Members of the military may spend months living on aircraft carriers. Water represents different things to different people. For residents of water cities, it may mean recreation, work, safety, or a way of life. It may also mean a connection to nature or the rest of the world. Earth’s water cities are proof that people can make a home for themselves just about anywhere.
pages.brief: A brightly colored fishing town in Italy clings to steep, rocky cliffs; in Northern California, a floating community is made of different kinds of houseboats; and members of the military live for months on an aircraft carrier, showing several more kinds of water cities.

books.title: The Story of Plastic
books.art_why: Keyword guidance points to drawing for this illustrated history-and-environment book.

pages.text: Plastic bottles are light, strong, and cheap. The Convenience of Plastic The Convenience of Plastic In 2016, people around the world bought more than 480 billion plastic drinking bottles. That figure equals almost 70 bottles for each person on Earth. Every minute, more than a million plastic bottles are sold around the world. Disposable bottles are just one example of how we use plastic. This amazing material is everywhere. It’s lightweight and inexpensive, strong yet flexible, and can be molded into almost any shape for a million different purposes. Plastic products are all around us. Your computer keyboard? Your pen? Your candy bar wrapper? These and many other products are made of some type of plastic. We live in an age of plastic. This material is a modern-day wonder. It is also cause for growing concern as we consider what to do with all our plastic trash.
pages.brief: A bright tabletop holds a computer keyboard, a pen, a wrapped candy bar and a light plastic drink bottle. Behind it, a busy street shows many shoppers holding disposable bottles. Piles of bottles suggest the huge number sold every minute around the world.

pages.text: In 1907, Belgian American chemist Leo Baekeland accidentally invented the first completely synthetic plastic. Called Bakelite, the material could be formed into most any shape and then cooled into a hard, stiff form. It was the forerunner of such Bakelite popularized the use materials as plexiglass, of plastic in household goods. polyester, nylon, and vinyl. Bakelite was used to make telephones, radios, kitchenware, car parts, and thousands of other products. The word plastic itself, though, did not become popular until the 1930s. It comes from the Greek word plassein, which means “to mold or shape.” Plastic can be molded and shaped into almost anything, and chemists and material engineers are still finding new forms and uses for it. Do You Know? Leo Baekeland was trying to create a new chemical for coating furniture when he accidentally created Bakelite. Like Baekeland, many scientists have created important substances by accident. Charles Goodyear reportedly created weatherproof rubber after accidentally leaving a chemical mixture on a hot stove. Chemist Stephanie Kwolek came up with Kevlar, used in bulletproof vests, while working to develop a strong, lightweight fiber for tires.
pages.brief: In a 1907 laboratory, chemist Leo Baekeland stands beside molds and a cooling tray, shaping the first synthetic plastic into a hard form. Around him sit a telephone, a radio, kitchenware and car parts made from his Bakelite. The scene shows how the accidental invention spread into household goods.

pages.text: Cotton, wood, and latex from rubber trees are all natural polymers. Miracle Material Miracle Material Plastic is special because of its atomic structure. Atoms link together to form molecules—the tiny building blocks of all matter. Plastic is a polymer—a substance made of large molecules that are linked in repeating units. These molecules bond very strongly in long chains, making them difficult to break and therefore very durable. Cellulose, a material that forms the cell walls of plants, is a type of natural polymer. Most plastics today, though, are made from synthetic polymers that don’t occur in nature. Scientists are able to create these polymers using oil, natural gas, or chemicals that can be made from them. The chemicals are loaded with carbon atoms that form strong bonds with other atoms.
pages.brief: Cotton bolls, a wooden block and latex dripping from a rubber tree show natural polymers. Beside them, long chains of atoms link tightly in repeating units. A cutaway view of oil and natural gas underground shows the carbon-rich chemicals scientists use to create synthetic polymer chains.

pages.text: There are two types of plastics— thermosets and thermoplastics. Thermosets are hard and brittle, and can withstand heat. Once they are shaped and cooled, they cannot be remelted. Examples of thermoset plastic include bathroom tiles, countertops, and baking dishes. Thermoset countertop tiles are strong and heat resistant. Thermoplastics can stretch and can also be melted, reformed, and recycled fairly easily. Milk jugs, plastic storage containers, and most toys are examples of this kind of plastic. Thermoplastics make up more than 90 percent of plastic products we know and use. Plastic storage containers are light and strong.
pages.brief: A kitchen and bathroom display split into two groups. Bathroom tiles, a countertop and a baking dish show hard, heat-resistant thermoset plastic. Milk jugs, clear storage containers and colorful toys show thermoplastic that can stretch, melt and be reformed. The containers look light and strong.

pages.text: Plastic has largely replaced leather and cloth as the main material used in athletic shoes. The Case for Plastic The Case for Plastic In the past century, plastic became the shape- shifting wonder of manufacturers’ dreams. Wood, metal, stone, glass, and ceramics can be fragile and difficult to work with. Plastic, on the other hand, can be molded with great precision to meet the needs and wishes of businesses and consumers. Plastic is easy to make and transform, and has come to represent convenience. It is the plastic bottle we drink from, the toothbrush we use to clean our teeth, and the disposable plates we picnic on and toss away. Plastic has also proven its value in other ways we may not notice.
pages.brief: A pair of athletic shoes made mostly of plastic sits beside a plastic drink bottle, a toothbrush and disposable picnic plates. A manufacturer's mold shows plastic being shaped with precision. The scene suggests how plastic replaced leather and cloth and became a convenient everyday material.

pages.text: Plastic helps make cars more lightweight and saves fuel. One example of plastic’s benefits is energy savings. Builders use plastics to insulate homes, schools, and office buildings. Insulation saves energy by keeping heat in on cold days and keeping heat out when the thermometer climbs. Plastic is also lighter than glass or any other material that might be used for packaging. The lighter weight saves fuel when shipping goods. In a similar way, plastic parts have helped reduce the weight of cars, trucks, aircraft, and other forms of transport. The less a vehicle weighs, the less fuel it needs to move. In turn, lower manufacturing and shipping costs save money for shoppers. Most plastic products can also be mass-produced more efficiently and cheaply than products made from other materials, again reducing costs for consumers. Plastic packaging also reduces food waste by keeping meat, bread, and vegetables fresh for longer periods. Plastic has proven to be good business for manufacturers, retailers, and customers.
pages.brief: A cutaway house, school and office building show plastic insulation keeping heat inside on a cold day. Nearby, lightweight plastic packaging surrounds fresh meat, bread and vegetables. A car, truck and aircraft use plastic parts to reduce weight, while shoppers pay less at a store.

pages.text: Any visit to a hospital or doctor’s office demonstrates plastic’s value to health care. Operating rooms are packed with plastic equipment, from monitors to tubes to surgical instruments. Plastic is easy to clean and resists contamination. Cheap, disposable supplies like syringes, examination gloves, and patient gowns reduce costs as well as the chances of infection. Cheap to make, lightweight, durable, versatile —these are the big reasons we have found so many uses for plastic in our lives. Disposable plastic medical supplies help keep doctors and patients safe in hospitals but create a large amount of plastic trash.

The clean room shows how cheap plastic supplies help protect patients, while a bin of used supplies hints at the trash they create.

The Problem with Plastic The Problem with Plastic Plastic has proven to be a miracle material, but more and more its drawbacks are there for all of us to see. A glance into a full dumpster reveals the problem—plastic trash. Plastic is turning into an environmental disaster. A plastic bottle of water can be a cool, refreshing drink, but it comes at a price. More than four hundred years from now, that plastic bottle will likely still be on Earth, perhaps buried in a landfill or lying on the seafloor.

pages.text: Plastic’s durability presents huge environmental challenges. Most food, wood, paper, and other plant materials break down over time and can be reused by nature. Plastic is different, though. Because most plastic is made from petrochemicals, natural forces cannot break it down easily, if at all. Over time, a plastic object may break into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics, but it never completely disappears. The low cost of making plastic also adds to the problem. It is cheaper to make new plastic bottles and other products than to reuse or recycle them. Many communities in the United States have recycling programs, but less than 10 percent of plastic is recycled, while another 15 percent is burned for energy. More than 75 percent of plastic is trucked to landfills or ends up dumped in the ocean. Plastic trash is not just ugly; biologists have proven that plastic is harming and killing wildlife. Dead whales have washed ashore with their guts stuffed with plastic bags they have mistakenly swallowed, thinking they were jellyfish or other food. Many seabirds are dying after swallowing plastic bits, and researchers are finding microplastics in fish, oysters, and other seafood we eat.

The scene shows how plastic breaks into smaller pieces but never disappears, harming wildlife and entering seafood.

Some countries are experimenting with charging customers a small deposit on each plastic drink bottle; they then get that money back when the container is returned. Norway’s “Deposit Return Scheme” has resulted in 96 percent of that country’s plastic bottles being recycled instead of becoming garbage. pages.text: Inventing a New Future for Plastic Inventing a New Future for Plastic Plastic is here to stay for many, many reasons. Plastic products make our daily lives easier, more affordable, and more convenient. Chemical engineers and inventors used their creative genius and worked hard to create a material that has so many good uses. Now, similar minds need to embrace the challenge of creating new forms of plastic that do less harm to the environment. In the meantime, we all can take action to be more mindful of our plastic habits. We need no special talents or knowledge to reduce our use of plastic, reuse it when possible, and recycle it at every opportunity— while still enjoying its benefits. Biodegradable Plastic? Plastic makers are working to create biodegradable plastics. These plastics are designed to break down naturally from exposure to weather or by means of chemicals released by microorganisms. books.art_why: It covers ice-age glaciers and an 1800s traveler, so drawn scenes suit the historical parts.

pages.text: This forested biome is mostly uninhabited. A Carpet of Green If you look down on Earth from a satellite high above the North Pole, you’ll see the Arctic Ocean. The first ring of land surrounding the North Pole is the treeless tundra region. Beyond the tundra lies a wider ring of deep green that is mostly empty of roads and cities. This region is home to an amazing number of trees as well as some hardiest of Earth’s animals. It remains nearly taiga untouched by modern life. This region is the. Sources disagree on the meaning of the Russian word taiga. Some say it means “forest-covered mountain,” while others believe it means “swampy, moist forest” or “coniferous forests.” In North America, the taiga is often referred to as the boreal forest. Boreal, which means “northern,” comes from Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind.
pages.brief: A satellite view high above the North Pole shows the Arctic Ocean surrounded by a ring of treeless tundra, then a wider deep-green ring of taiga forest across northern land. The taiga has many trees and hardy animals, with almost no roads or cities visible.

pages.text: Earth’s Taiga Regions EUROPE NORTH ASIA AMERICA AFRICA SOUTH AMERICA AUSTRALIA ANTARCTICA The Russian taiga measures about 5,800 kilometers (3,600 mi.) from east to west. The taiga—Earth’s largest land biome—occurs in a wide band across northern regions of North America, Europe, and Asia. In North America, much of Canada and Alaska are taiga. In Europe, the taiga occurs in small patches in the Highlands of Scotland. It then stretches from Norway, Sweden, and Finland all across Russia to the Pacific Ocean. It also extends into parts of China and Mongolia. About one-sixth of Earth’s land is taiga. To the north is the tundra, where almost no trees grow. The border between the two biomes is known as the tree line. Just south of the taiga, some parts of the world have temperate forests, while others have grasslands.
pages.brief: A world view shows a wide green band of taiga across northern North America, Europe and Asia, stretching from Norway and Finland across Russia to the Pacific. North of it lies treeless tundra at the tree line; south are temperate forests and grasslands. The Russian taiga reaches about 5,800 kilometers east to west.

pages.text: Climate and Soil The climate in the taiga is typically cold, although it varies from place to place. Because of the taiga’s location far north of the equator, sunlight strikes the land at a low angle. As a result, this region receives less heat energy than places nearer the equator. Snow cover also contributes to the cold by reflecting sunlight instead of absorbing it. A third factor is the taiga’s long winter nights, which allow more heat to escape into Earth’s atmosphere. Winters in the taiga are long, cold, and windy. Temperatures are usually below −10°C (14°F) in January, the coldest month. In eastern Siberia, winter temperatures have dropped as low as −50°C (−58°F). Accumulated snow generally lasts all winter—five months or more in the southern taiga and up to eight months in the northern taiga. Glaciers and Land Bridges Much of the taiga was covered with glaciers during the last ice age, which ended just under twelve thousand years ago. With so much of Earth’s water frozen, sea levels remained lower. As a result, many of today’s islands, such as the British Isles, were connected to the mainland above water. A land bridge between the far eastern part of Russia and parts of Alaska and Canada allowed many animal species to move to North America.
pages.brief: A cold winter taiga under a low sun, with deep snow reflecting light, windblown trees and a dark sky suggesting long winter night. In the distance, glaciers and a land bridge connect far eastern Russia with Alaska and Canada.

pages.text: Skies are deep purple during a foggy thunderstorm in the Canadian taiga. July, the warmest month, ranges between 15 and 20°C (59–68°F) and may even reach 25°C (77°F) during the hottest time of the day. Frequent thunderstorms with lightning and low rainfall can cause forest fires during warmer months. Fires can be useful because they remove old and sick trees and make room for new ones to grow. Annual precipitation in the taiga is highest in eastern North America and northern Europe, which have many lakes, streams, and wetlands. These areas may receive over 100 centimeters (39 in.) of precipitation each year.
pages.brief: A foggy thunderstorm over the Canadian taiga, with deep purple sky and lightning above dense forest. Warm summer air and low rainfall allow a forest fire to burn among old trees. Nearby lakes, streams and wetlands hold heavy precipitation in eastern North America and northern Europe.

pages.text: Soils in the taiga are generally rocky, and nutrient poor. This limits the types of plants Spruce and tamarack trees, along with mosses and other plants, grow in boggy areas. that can grow in many places. In warmer areas of the taiga, soils contain more nutrients because organic matter breaks down more quickly. In many parts of Canada, glaciers have scraped the land, leaving the soil too thin for mature forests to grow. Permafrost—permanently frozen ground— or else solid rock lies just below the surface soil in many areas. Neither one allows soil to drain well. For this reason, the taiga has many shallow bogs. Climate change is creating more bogs as the permafrost melts. Permafrost in the Taiga Areas of the taiga with below-freezing average annual temperatures may contain permafrost. Many species of trees are unable to grow in these areas, but some, including tamarack and black spruce, can still thrive if the layer of surface soil above the frozen ground is deep enough. Permafrost is common in northern Canada and the Asian portion of Russia. It tends to occur in areas that receive less sunlight, such as the north side of mountain slopes.
pages.brief: A boggy taiga area with shallow pools, mosses, spruce and tamarack trees growing in rocky, nutrient-poor soil. Solid rock or permafrost lies just below the surface, so water drains poorly. Melting permafrost is creating more shallow bogs in northern Canada and Asian Russia.

pages.text: Taiga Plants Plants in the taiga must survive a short growing season as well as cold temperatures, permafrost, and nutrient- poor soil. As a result, fewer species grow there than in biomes at lower Scotch pine is one of the most latitudes. The main common trees found in the taiga. plants are conifers, including pine, fir, and spruce. Many of these trees are evergreens, which keep their leaves year-round. But tamarack, another common conifer, is deciduous, dropping its leaves in winter. Some flower-bearing deciduous trees, such as poplar and birch, also grow in the taiga, although they’re less widespread. Much of the ground cover is mosses, lichens, and mushrooms, which have shallow roots. They don’t require much sunlight or water, and they can bear the cold. Some grasses, ferns, and other low plants also grow in the taiga. Calypso orchids grow in damp areas of the taiga during summer.
pages.brief: A summer taiga scene with Scotch pine, fir and spruce trees, some evergreen and some tamarack dropping leaves. Poplar and birch trees grow nearby. Mosses, lichens, mushrooms, grasses and ferns cover the ground with shallow roots, and Calypso orchids bloom in a damp area.

pages.text: Plants have several important adaptations for surviving in the taiga. Keeping their leaves all year helps evergreen trees conserve energy and nutrients. Growing new leaves in spring would require Scotch pine needles conserve water more sunlight and soil (top). A Norway spruce withstands heavy snowfall (bottom). nutrients, both of which are in short supply. Many cone-bearing trees in the taiga, such as pines, have needlelike leaves with a waxy coating. This leaf design allows trees to conserve water, which may be scarce due to low rainfall or because it’s frozen. Needles also protect trees from freezing since they don’t contain much sap. Dark-green leaves increase heat absorption and help trees take in the Sun’s energy for use in photosynthesis. Many trees are cone shaped, with branches that shed snow quickly so the snow’s weight doesn’t break them.
pages.brief: Close view of taiga trees in snow: a Scotch pine with waxy needlelike leaves conserving water, and a cone-shaped Norway spruce with branches shedding heavy snowfall. Dark-green evergreen needles absorb heat and sunlight, helping the trees make food through photosynthesis.

pages.text: Taiga Animals The cold climate and restricted types of plants limit the kinds of animals that can live in the taiga. Animals there are hardy and well adapted to the challenging conditions. Mammals tend to grow thick fur for insulation, and larger species often have long legs and large feet to navigate in deep snow. The biome’s large herbivores include deer, elk, moose, and caribou (also known as reindeer). Predators include black and grizzly bears, wolves, wolverines, lynxes, and weasel-like martens, as well as Siberian tigers in eastern Russia. Squirrels, snowshoe hares, and lemmings are among the smaller mammals. Birds of prey, including eagles, hawks, and owls, hunt them from trees.
pages.brief: A snowy taiga with thick-furred mammals: moose, caribou, deer and elk among trees; a grizzly bear, wolf, wolverine, lynx and Siberian tiger; squirrels, snowshoe hare and lemmings. Eagles, hawks and owls hunt from trees, while larger animals use long legs and big feet in deep snow.

pages.text: Enormous numbers of insects breed in bogs, lakes, and ponds in the summer. Waterfowl and many other kinds of birds migrate to the taiga to take advantage of this plentiful food source and raise their young. These birds migrate south to warmer regions during the long, cold winters. Woodpeckers, ravens, loons, and chickadees are year-round residents. The taiga is a challenging biome for reptiles and amphibians, which can’t regulate their body temperature internally. In spring and summer, some parts of the taiga are warm enough for these animals. They cope with the cold by hibernating in winter, either on land or, in the case of turtles and some frogs, at the bottom of lakes and ponds. Frozen Frogs Wood frogs survive the taiga’s cold with the help of an unusual adaptation: their blood and body tissues freeze while they hibernate. In this frozen state, their breathing and heartbeat stop, blood ceases to flow, and ice crystals form under their skin. Special proteins and sugars protect their cells from damage. These frogs can tolerate more than half of their body freezing.
pages.brief: Summer taiga ponds and bogs swarm with insects. Migrating waterfowl and other birds feed and raise young, while woodpeckers, ravens, loons and chickadees stay year-round. Frogs and turtles hibernate at the bottom of a pond; a wood frog lies frozen with ice crystals under its skin.
