Many of these people are working This woman is a tribal elder of the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi in Quebec. to preserve both Her tribe is one of the most active the forests and their native groups working to protect the taiga in Canada. traditional way of life. Because the taiga is forested, trees are a key natural resource, and logging is widespread. Mining, oil and gas exploration, and road construction are other industrial activities in this biome. People also travel to the taiga to enjoy boating, fishing, hiking, skiing, snowmobiling, dogsledding, and relaxing in cozy cabins. Most of the taiga is fairly unpopulated. The two largest cities are Toronto, Canada, and Moscow, Russia.
pages.brief: A Cree First Nation tribal elder woman of Waswanipi in Quebec stands in the taiga, working to protect the forest and her people’s traditional life. Around her are fishing, hunting, crafts, logging, mining, roads and recreation like boating, hiking, skiing and dogsledding; distant Toronto and Moscow are the largest cities.

pages.text: One of the world’s largest taiga areas lies in Russia. Where Conifers Rule The taiga stretches nearly 13 million square kilometers (about 5 million sq. mi.) across Earth’s northern lands. Conifers reign supreme in this cold region. Siberia, in Russia, includes vast areas of taiga. Russian playwright Anton Chekhov traveled to the Siberian taiga on horseback in the late 1800s. He was so struck by the endless expanse of green conifers that he wondered if he’d ever get out. Although it’s certainly possible to leave the taiga, those fortunate enough to experience this land won’t soon forget it.
pages.brief: A vast Siberian taiga of endless green conifers stretches to the horizon under a wide sky. Russian playwright Anton Chekhov rides horseback through the late 1800s forest, small among the trees, looking out at the expanse and wondering if he will ever get out.

books.title: Lakes
books.art_why: Modern lakes, parks, and people today can be photographed.

pages.text: Healing Waters Being near water is healing. Recent scientific research confirms what people have likely known since the dawn of time. Water soothes us, calms our busy minds, inspires creativity, and gives rise to a sense of wonder. While all kinds of water can be healing, lakes and ponds have a character all their own. They generally have still water, which is quite different from wild ocean waves or the rush of a flowing river. If you’ve ever marveled at a landscape perfectly mirrored in a lake, you’ve experienced the calming power of lakes. Morning fog rises from a lake in Vermont’s Green Mountain National Forest.
pages.brief: A still lake in Vermont’s Green Mountain National Forest at morning, with fog rising from the water. Forested mountains surround the lake, and the calm surface reflects the landscape. No people are present; the scene focuses on the quiet water and mist.

pages.text: Lakes Around the World Lakes exist on every continent and within every land biome. Earth’s millions of lakes vary greatly in size and depth. The largest is the Caspian Sea, a saltwater lake. (Long ago, it was named a sea because it is huge and salty, but scientists generally consider it a lake.) The largest freshwater lake is Lake Superior, one of the Great Lakes, which are on the border between Canada and the United States. Although we often think of lakes as calm, large lakes such as the Great Lakes have strong currents and possess some of the characteristics of an ocean. Notable Lakes Around the World NORTH NORTH EUROPE EUROPE AMERICA AMERICA ASIA ASIA AFRICA AFRICA SOUTH SOUTH AMERICA AMERICA These are just a few of Earth’s best-known lakes.
pages.brief: A broad view of Earth’s lakes across every continent, with the Caspian Sea shown as a huge saltwater lake and Lake Superior as the largest freshwater lake on the Canada–United States border. The Great Lakes appear large, with strong currents and ocean-like traits.

pages.text: Formed in 1991, Lake Pinatubo, in the Philippines, is one of the world’s youngest crater lakes. At 2,000 feet, it is also the country’s deepest lake. How Lakes Form Lakes often form when low areas of land, called basins, fill with water. Lake basins can form in many different ways. The Great Lakes, along with many other lakes in the Northern Hemisphere, formed around fourteen thousand years ago at the end of the last ice age. Huge glaciers moved slowly, carving out basins and eroding the land. As they moved, they ground up the rock and sediment beneath them, creating tiny pieces called glacial flour. Water from melting glaciers later filled the basins. Volcanoes can also cause lake basins to form. After a volcano stops erupting, rain or melted snow can fill its crater. Water can also fill a caldera, a large depression formed when the top of a volcano collapses during a violent eruption.
pages.brief: Lake Pinatubo in the Philippines fills a volcanic crater, a young crater lake and the country’s deepest. Nearby, a glacier slowly carves a basin in the land, grinding rock into glacial flour; meltwater later fills the basin. A collapsed volcanic caldera also holds water.

pages.text: Plitvice (PLEET-veet-suh) Lakes National Park, in Croatia, has sixteen solution lakes connected by waterfalls. Some lakes form as a result of water dissolving certain types of underground rocks. Rocks made of limestone or salt are most likely to dissolve. Once they do, the ground above them lacks support, so it caves in and forms a lake. Rocks that dissolve are called soluble, which means “able to be dissolved,” and the lakes they form are called solution lakes. The movement of huge pieces of Earth’s crust deep underground can also create lake basins. Deep cracks called faults can form when these pieces move. Lake Baikal, in southern Russia, formed in this way. It is Earth’s deepest lake, with an estimated depth of 1,637 meters (5,369 ft.).
pages.brief: In Croatia’s Plitvice Lakes National Park, sixteen solution lakes are linked by waterfalls. Underground limestone and salt dissolve, leaving the ground above unsupported so it caves in and forms a lake. Elsewhere, a deep fault crack in southern Russia holds Lake Baikal, Earth’s deepest lake.

pages.text: Several types of lakes don’t begin as a basin that fills with water. Oxbow lakes, for example, are formed by river currents. Some rivers flow in a winding path. Erosion is greater on the outside of the bends, where the current is faster, than on the inside. Sediment builds up on the inside because water moves more slowly. Over time, those sediments cause a loop to close off and the river to follow a new path. The water that remains in the closed-off loop forms an oxbow lake. Landslides and mudslides can also form lakes. Rocks, soil, and mud that slide down a hill or valley can pile up, causing a stream’s flow to become blocked. Lakes that form in this manner are usually temporary. Small streams can also get blocked by beaver dams. People create artificial lakes, or reservoirs, when they build hydroelectric dams on rivers. Lakes are not permanent, even though they may seem to be, given our life span. Most lakes that exist today are less than twenty thousand years old. Lakes eventually turn into wetlands and later disappear completely. A few ancient lakes formed as a result of movement in Earth’s crust. The oldest, Lake Baikal, is at least twenty- five million years old.
pages.brief: A winding river cuts across land; faster current erodes the outside of a bend while sediment builds on the inside, eventually closing a loop into an oxbow lake. A landslide blocks a stream, a beaver dam stops a small stream, and a hydroelectric dam creates a reservoir. Lake Baikal endures as an ancient lake.

pages.text: Salt Lakes Scientists consider lakes to be either open or closed. Most water in open lakes leaves by flowing into a river or another body of water. The water in most closed lakes only leaves by evaporating. These lakes are salty, or saline, because when water evaporates, salt is left behind. Saline lakes are often surrounded by salt flats—areas where all the lake water has evaporated, leaving behind a thick layer of salt on the ground. Freshwater lakes contain very little salt—just 0.05 percent (5 parts per thousand [ppt]) or less. The amount of salt in ocean water is about 3.5 percent (35 ppt). The salt content in saline lakes can be greater than 30 percent (300 ppt), although it varies a great deal. The largest saline lake in the Western Hemisphere is Great Salt Lake, in Utah. Its salinity ranges between 6 and 30 percent (60–300 ppt). The Dead Sea, a saline lake in the Middle East, has a salt content of 33.7 percent (337 ppt). One of the saltiest lakes on Earth is Don Juan Pond, which is located in Antarctica. Its salinity can be as great as 44 percent (440 ppt). Because of the high salt content, the pond doesn’t freeze unless the surrounding temperature drops below –50 degrees Celsius (–58°F). It’s easy to float in salt water, such as that found in Utah’s Great Salt Lake (shown here). The higher the salt content, the denser the water. The denser the water, the higher you float!
pages.brief: A person floats easily in Utah’s Great Salt Lake, where high salinity makes the water dense. Around a closed saline lake, salt flats remain after water evaporates. The Dead Sea and Antarctica’s Don Juan Pond hold extremely salty water; Don Juan Pond stays liquid unless the surrounding temperature falls below –50°C.

pages.text: Lake Zones and Organisms Sunlight often reaches all the way down to the bottom of shallow lakes and ponds. In contrast, deep lakes and ponds have zones that differ with regard to light, wind, and temperature. The littoral zone is the part of a lake closest to the shore. It has the shallowest, warmest water. Both the water and the soil beneath it receive plenty of sunlight, which allows plants and algae to live there. Some plants, such as cattails and reeds, are rooted and stick out above the surface of the water. Other rooted plants, including pondweed, grow completely underwater. Perhaps the best-known plants in the littoral zone are rooted plants with floating leaves, such as water lilies. Other plants, such as duckweed, float freely on the water. Many animals make their homes in littoral zone plants. These small fish. Many also lay eggs A great blue heron hunts for fish in the on the plants. littoral zone.
pages.brief: In the shallow, warm littoral zone near a lake’s shore, sunlight reaches the bottom. Cattails and reeds stand above the surface, pondweed grows underwater, water lilies float rooted leaves, and duckweed drifts freely. Small fish hide and lay eggs among the plants while a great blue heron hunts for fish.

pages.text: Lake Zones The limnetic zone is the open water near the surface in the middle of a lake. Like the littoral zone, it receives plentiful sunlight and supports plant growth. Microscopic organisms known as phytoplankton and zooplankton live here, along with many fish. The water contains a lot of oxygen. The profundal zone, located below the limnetic zone, is colder. Because of its depth, it doesn’t receive sunlight. Fewer fish live here because oxygen levels are low during certain seasons. The benthic zone is the sediment at the bottom of a lake. Most of this zone is cold and dark. Worms, clams, and other animals live here and are food for certain kinds of fish. Dead organic matter from other zones falls to the benthic zone, where it is broken down by bacteria.
pages.brief: A cross-section of a lake shows the open, sunlit limnetic zone in the middle, where phytoplankton, zooplankton, and fish live in oxygen-rich water. Below it, the colder profundal zone receives no sunlight and has fewer fish. At the bottom, the cold, dark benthic zone holds worms and clams, and dead matter falls to bacteria.

pages.text: Lakes support many animals that aren’t strictly aquatic. Frogs, salamanders, turtles, muskrats, otters, beavers, alligators, loons, ducks, geese, herons, and others require both land and water habitats. Lakes also provide food for visiting animals, such as moose, raccoons, and migrating birds. In addition, ponds are breeding grounds for many different kinds of organisms, and lake plants offer hidden places to raise babies. In winter, lakes and ponds freeze from top to bottom. Because most never freeze solid, many organisms are able to survive winter in deep water. Each year, hundreds of thousands of flamingos gather on Lakes Bogoria and Nakuru in Kenya, East Africa, to feed on algae and raise chicks.
pages.brief: At a lake edge, frogs, salamanders, turtles, muskrats, otters, beavers, alligators, loons, ducks, geese, and herons share land and water. A moose and raccoons visit for food while migrating birds stop by. In Kenya, hundreds of thousands of flamingos gather on Lakes Bogoria and Nakuru to feed on algae and raise chicks.

pages.text: People and Lakes Lakes and ponds have been important to people since ancient times. Ships have crossed large lakes for travel and trade. Farmers have used the water in lakes and ponds to irrigate their crops. Today, lakes supply much of our drinking water as well as water to cool power plants, steel mills, and chemical plants. Reservoirs store water that can be used in case of drought. Lakes also provide plentiful opportunities for recreation. Fishing, boating, swimming, and water-skiing bring thousands of people to lakes each year. Camping, hiking, photography, and watching wildlife are also popular, as are ice- skating and ice fishing in winter. A mother fishes with her daughter in Wyoming’s Bighorn Mountains.
pages.brief: A mother fishes with her daughter beside a lake in Wyoming’s Bighorn Mountains. Around the lake, people use water for drinking and irrigation, reservoirs store water for drought, and boats cross for travel and trade. Others swim, water-ski, camp, hike, photograph wildlife, or ice-fish in winter.

pages.text: The last light of day is reflected in Maligne (muh-LEEN) Lake, the longest and deepest lake in the Canadian Rockies. Peace and Beauty When we think about how lakes form, we are reminded that our planet is constantly changing. Yet the glassy surface of a secluded lake shows us that nature can also be serene. Lakes invite us to take comfort in the beauty of wild places. They also call on us to slow down and pay attention to our surroundings. The American writer Henry David Thoreau was so inspired by that call that he left his regular life in Concord, Massachusetts, to live alone at Walden Pond for two years. During that time, he lived simply, while studying nature and writing about it. In his words, “A lake is the landscape’s most beautiful and expressive feature. It is earth’s eye; looking into which the beholder measures the depth of his own nature.”
pages.brief: The last light of day reflects on Maligne Lake, the longest and deepest lake in the Canadian Rockies. The glassy surface lies quiet among wild mountains, showing a serene side of a constantly changing planet. The scene invites viewers to slow down and take comfort in the beauty of a secluded lake.

pages.text: Welcome to Ukraine Ukraine became an independent country in 1991, making it one of the youngest countries in the world. Yet it has a long and fascinating history. Because of its rich soil, one of the world’s first civilizations to practice agriculture developed there more than five thousand years ago. Some of the castles and cities you can visit in Ukraine today have been standing for more than one thousand years. Due to its location, various empires fought to control it for centuries. Today, the cultural influence of these empires can be seen in Ukraine’s art, cuisine, and architecture. From delicious food to medieval castles and lively music festivals, there is so much to see and experience in Ukraine! A group of people wear traditional Ukrainian clothing during a march in the city of Kyiv.
pages.brief: In Kyiv, a group of people wearing traditional Ukrainian clothing march together through the city. Their outfits and public procession show cultural pride, and the scene places them in Ukraine’s capital during a lively community event.

pages.text: Ukraine is the world’s biggest producer of sunflower oil, a popular oil for cooking. Besides the Carpathian Mountains in the west and the Crimean Mountains on the peninsula, most of Ukraine is flat. Summers are often warm and humid, while winters are cold and dry. The fertile soil and mild weather of the country’s plains make the land ideal for growing wheat. Because of this, Ukraine is sometimes referred to as the “breadbasket of Europe.” Wheat, corn, sunflowers, potatoes, and sugar beets are some of the main crops grown there. Synevir Lake is a popular destination for visitors.
pages.brief: Synevir Lake is shown as a popular destination for visitors, with water and surrounding land. Nearby fields contain wheat, corn, sunflowers, potatoes, and sugar beets, crops grown in Ukraine’s fertile soil, while distant mountains rise in the west and on the Crimean peninsula.

pages.text: The People Although Ukraine is twice the size of Italy, it has about seventeen million fewer people. More than two-thirds of the country’s population lives in cities. Kyiv (KI-yeev), the capital of Ukraine, is the largest city. Nearly three million people live there. Most people in the country are native Ukrainians, with Russians making up the next largest group. Ukrainians are part of an ethnic group called Slavs—people primarily from central and eastern Europe who speak a Slavic language. Kyiv is one of the oldest cities in Eastern Europe. It was founded in 482 ce— more than 1,500 years ago.
pages.brief: People are shown in Kyiv, the capital and largest city of Ukraine, where nearly three million residents live. The city is presented as one of Eastern Europe’s oldest, founded in 482 CE, and as a major urban center for the country’s population.

pages.text: Elementary school students in Ukraine practice their reading skills. Most people in Ukraine speak Ukrainian. Many other languages are spoken as well, including Russian, Polish, and Yiddish (a language spoken by some Jewish people in Europe). Today, Ukrainian is the official language of the country, but that wasn’t always the case. In fact, at various times throughout the country’s history, the language was banned in schools, churches, theaters, and other public institutions. For a while, it was even against the law to publish books in Ukrainian or give babies Ukrainian names. Ukrainian became the country’s official language once again in 1989.
pages.brief: Elementary school students in Ukraine sit together and practice their reading skills, holding books in a classroom. The scene reflects how most people in Ukraine speak Ukrainian, while other languages such as Russian, Polish, and Yiddish are also spoken.

pages.text: History Humans have lived in Ukraine since prehistoric times. In the 8th century bce—around 2,750 years ago—groups of people from what is now Iran settled in the plains. In the following centuries, Greeks established colonies along the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. Around the same time, Slavs were migrating from their homeland north of the Carpathian Mountains to settle throughout the region. They built settlements that later developed into important centers for business and politics. Kyiv grew out of one of these early settlements. By the 11th century ce, the Slavs had joined with Viking invaders from Scandinavia and formed a powerful kingdom called Kyivan Rus. It was the largest empire in Europe at the time. The empire’s reign ended when the Mongols arrived from central Asia and attacked the kingdom in the 1200s. Lithuania then took control of most of Ukraine in the 1300s. These are the ruins of the ancient city of Tauric Chersonese, built around 422 bce.
pages.brief: The ruins of the ancient city of Tauric Chersonese stand near the Black Sea, built around 422 BCE. The stone remains show an early settlement in Ukraine’s long history, from a time before the Kyivan Rus kingdom and later invasions by Mongols and Lithuania.

pages.text: The Kamianets-Podilskyi Castle is thought to have been built in the 13th or 14th century. In the late 1500s, Poland invaded Ukraine. The Polish forced most Ukrainians to become serfs— farmers who were obligated to work on land they didn’t own. Serfs had little wealth or power. Angry over their situation, the serfs rebelled in the 1600s. They formed a military force called the Cossacks and asked for Russia’s help in defeating the Polish. The Cossacks won independence from Poland, but by the late 1700s, Russia had gained control of nearly all of Ukraine. It was during this time that use of the Ukrainian language was prohibited. By 1922, Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union, the largest country to ever exist. It included what are now the separate countries of Lithuania, Belarus, Russia, and Moldova, among many others. The Soviet Union broke apart in 1991, and Ukraine declared its independence. That year, the country elected its first president, Leonid Kravchuk.
pages.brief: The Kamianets-Podilskyi Castle, thought to have been built in the 13th or 14th century, stands as a historic fortress in Ukraine. Its walls and towers represent the many rulers and conflicts that shaped the country, from Polish control and Cossack rebellion to Russian rule and Soviet power.

pages.text: The Chernobyl Disaster In April 1986, explosions at a nuclear power station in Chernobyl (chair-NOH-bil) released radioactive material into the air. Radioactive materials give off a form of energy called radiation, which can be dangerous to living creatures in high amounts. Wind carried the radioactive material as far west as France and Italy, exposing hundreds of thousands of people and millions of acres of land to harmful radiation. Following the accident, thousands of people were forced to leave their homes. The government made it illegal to come within 30 kilometers (18 mi.) of the nuclear power station because the land, water, and air had become radioactive. The radiation had also caused deformities—misshapen or abnormal body parts—in animals born near the site. To this day, no people live there because the land and animals are still radioactive. Landmarks Ukraine has many incredible landmarks, both natural and human-made. It has more than forty- five national parks, including the Carpathian National Nature Park, which was established in 1980 to protect the landscapes of the Carpathian Mountains. Mount Hoverla (hoh-VAIR-lah), the tallest mountain in Ukraine, is there. Another popular park is the Oleshky Sands National Nature Park in southern Ukraine, which contains 1,620 square kilometers The Sun rises on a misty (625 sq. mi.) of sand dunes. morning in the Carpathian That’s twice the size of Kyiv! Mountains.
pages.brief: The sun rises on a misty morning in the Carpathian Mountains, within the Carpathian National Nature Park, established in 1980. Mount Hoverla, Ukraine’s tallest mountain, is there. The park protects the mountain landscapes that are among Ukraine’s natural landmarks.

pages.text: Ukraine is home to many castles, palaces, monasteries, and cathedrals. One popular destination for visitors is the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra (peh-CHAIRSK LAHV-rah), also known as the Kiev Monastery of the Caves. The monastery is one of Ukraine’s seven World Heritage Sites— places considered important to world history. It was founded in 1051 ce. Beneath it lies caves and catacombs—underground burial sites—which contain important religious relics, as well as the bodies of monks mummified and preserved in glass coffins. Khotyn Fortress Another important Ukrainian landmark is the Khotyn (HOH-tin) fortress located in Khotyn, one of the oldest towns in Ukraine. The structure, originally made of wood, was probably built in the early 11th century, though different rulers have added to it over time. It’s one of the oldest preserved fortifications—structures built to defend an area against attacks—in Eastern Europe. This is probably because a wall nearly 6 meters (20 ft.) thick and over 40 meters (130 ft.) high was added to it in the 1400s, making it strong enough to withstand cannon fire. The fortress is one of more than five thousand fortifications in Ukraine.
pages.brief: Khotyn Fortress stands in Khotyn, one of Ukraine’s oldest towns. Its massive wall, nearly 6 meters thick and over 40 meters high, was added in the 1400s and made the fortification strong enough to withstand cannon fire.

pages.text: Ukraine’s Tunnel of Love One of the most popular places to visit in Ukraine is the Tunnel of Love, a 4-kilometer (2.5 mi.) natural tunnel that surrounds a train track in the city of Klevan. Trees were planted on either side of the tracks in the 1940s to hide trains heading to an army base. Over time, the trees’ branches formed arches across the tracks. Today, the tunnel’s beauty draws visitors from all over the world. Celebrations Ukraine has many celebrations throughout the year. One of the most important is Independence Day on August 24. This holiday marks the day Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. It is celebrated in cities throughout the country with concerts, festivals, and parades. People carry the Ukrainian flag during a parade to celebrate Independence Day.
pages.brief: People carry the Ukrainian flag during a parade in a Ukrainian city to celebrate Independence Day on August 24. The holiday marks the day Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, and it is celebrated with concerts, festivals, and parades throughout the country.

pages.text: A girl wearing traditional Ukrainian clothing puts a crown of wildflowers on her head. Like many countries, Ukraine also has holidays to celebrate the seasons. One is Ivan Kupala Day, which marks the beginning of summer. There are many traditions associated with this holiday, including dancing around a bonfire, making wildflower wreaths, and bathing in lakes. Masliana is a week-long holiday celebrating the end of winter and the arrival of spring. Many traditional dishes eaten during this week are made with cheese and butter. Two of the most popular dishes are varenyky (vah-REH-nih-kih), or dumplings, and pancakes. Long ago, people believed that the more fun they had during this holiday, the more successful the following year would be, so it is often celebrated with lots of music, entertainment, and food.
pages.brief: A girl wearing traditional Ukrainian clothing places a crown of wildflowers on her head. The scene connects to Ivan Kupala Day, a summer holiday with traditions such as dancing around a bonfire, making wildflower wreaths, and bathing in lakes.

pages.text: Conclusion Ukraine is home to incredible landscapes, beautiful architecture, and vibrant cities that attract millions of visitors each year. The country has a long, sometimes difficult history, because it was ruled by many different empires and rulers for centuries before finally gaining its independence. But throughout Ukraine’s history, its people maintained their language and culture. Even today, annual celebrations keep centuries-old traditions alive. From stunning national parks to joyful festivals, the country of Ukraine has a lot to offer. A woman holds Ukraine’s national flag.
pages.brief: A woman holds Ukraine’s national flag, standing as a symbol of the country’s independence. The scene reflects Ukraine’s incredible landscapes, beautiful architecture, vibrant cities, long history, and annual celebrations that keep centuries-old traditions alive today.

books.title: Ships of Discovery
books.art_why: Historical ships and voyages predate photography, so drawn illustrations are needed.

pages.text: Introduction People often settle along rivers, lakes, and seas where they can find fresh water, nutrient-rich soil, and bountiful fishing. Long ago, people who lived near large bodies of water were curious about what might exist beyond the horizon. They also speculated that traveling over water might be easier than traveling over land. They noticed that particular materials, such as wood, reeds, or skins full of air, were buoyant. These thoughts led to the construction of the first simple boat. As boats and ships became more practical, people were able to travel farther from home. Advancing technology created new types of boats that were able to carry more cargo and were often safer, faster, and more comfortable. Boats became important tools for commerce, exploration, and defense. Let’s examine how boats were used to explore the world and how they have changed over time.
pages.brief: People live beside rivers, lakes, and seas with fresh water, rich soil, and fish. They look past the horizon and wonder about travel over water. Wood, reeds, and air-filled skins float, leading to a first simple boat. Better boats carry more cargo and become safer, faster, and more comfortable for commerce, exploration, and defense.

pages.text: Over time, people wanted to transport larger cargoes over waterways. It became necessary to construct boats that could carry many people for long voyages. They also needed to be able to carry food, animals, and other items to trade. Canoes carved from a single oak tree and steered with a pole were adequate boats for crossing a lake or going down a river, but they didn’t work well for carrying bulky objects. Imagine trying to row a narrow canoe across a wide lake with six sheep crammed around you. The space just wasn’t sufficient. Humans have always strived to perfect and upgrade their inventions, so it was natural that ancient people searched for methods to build bigger, faster, and safer boats. People realized that they needed better boats if they were going to explore places far from their homeland.
pages.brief: People need boats that carry larger cargoes and many people on long voyages. A canoe carved from one oak tree and steered with a pole works on a lake or river, but not for bulky objects. Six sheep crammed around a rower show the space problem. Ancient people seek bigger, faster, safer boats for exploration.

pages.text: The next evolution in boat building was the use of wooden beams to make a frame. The frame was covered with wooden planks or bark from trees. Some cultures even used animal skins stretched over the frame to create a hull, the outer shell of a boat. These boats were bigger than previous designs, but were also more streamlined and able to hold more cargo. People also developed paddles and oars to move in deep water, where poles could not reach the bottom. The Egyptians were the first people to cover wooden frames with long, flat pieces of wood to create hulls. Some of their boats measured as much as 21.3 meters (70 ft) long. The Egyptians were also the first to use sails to harness the power of the wind. The use of sails eliminated or reduced the need for people to row the boats. Some boats used both rowers and sails.
pages.brief: Boat builders make a wooden-beam frame and cover it with planks, bark, or animal skins to form a hull. These boats are bigger, streamlined, and hold more cargo. Paddles and oars reach deep water. Egyptians cover wooden frames with long, flat wood pieces, build boats up to 21.3 meters long, and use sails to harness wind power.

pages.text: Soon, the Greeks, Phoenicians, and other peoples around the Mediterranean Sea were building large boats powered by sails. About 3,000 years ago, sailing ships were built with two masts, each one holding a sail. The addition of a second mast made a ship much easier to steer and also made it much faster. Five hundred years later, the Greeks developed a ship with four sails. This ship was safe enough to leave the Mediterranean Sea and travel down the west coast of Africa. Some of the fastest ships at the time were built for battle. These warships often had as many as three levels of rowers on each side of the ship. Arranging the rowers above each other on separate tiers provided a great deal of power in a small amount of space. Greek ships with three tiers of rowers were called triremes. These larger ships allowed people to travel to and explore distant places, and it was during this period that exploration and trade moved beyond the Mediterranean Sea. Although ocean travel still had its dangers, it had become safe enough that some brave explorers and traders dared to risk it.
pages.brief: Greeks, Phoenicians, and other Mediterranean peoples build large sailing ships. About 3,000 years ago ships have two masts, each holding a sail, making steering easier and travel faster. Five hundred years later Greek ships carry four sails and can leave the Mediterranean. Fast warships with three tiers of rowers, called triremes, help explorers and traders reach distant places.

pages.text: The Polynesians In the South Pacific, groups of Pacific Island peoples were building boats that could sail in the open ocean. Over 3,500 years ago, these people were traveling east, well beyond the archipelago of islands where they lived. They also explored areas off the Asian mainland. More than a thousand years ago, these people made journeys of thousands of miles in open boats. These Polynesian sailors built a type of boat that was an early version of the modern catamaran. They took two canoes and connected them using large wooden poles. A deck was then built to span the poles. These boats usually measured about 15 to 18 meters (50–60 ft) long. The central deck held masts for sails and had enough space for several people and their supplies for the duration of a lengthy voyage. Polynesian catamaran.
pages.brief: In the South Pacific, Pacific Island peoples build boats for the open ocean. More than a thousand years ago they travel thousands of miles. Their early catamaran joins two canoes with large wooden poles and a deck across them. The boats are about 15 to 18 meters long, with masts for sails and space for people and supplies.

pages.text: PACIFIC OCEAN ASIA Hawaiian Islands Easter AUSTRALIA Island New Zealand Routes of Polynesian expansion These early boats provided safe travel from one island to another. The Polynesians settled many new islands they discovered. By 1000 ce, they lived on nearly every habitable island they could find in the Pacific Ocean. Their new homes included Hawai ‘ i, New Zealand, and Rapa Nui (Easter Island). The Polynesians were accomplished sailors. They became so familiar with the ocean that they could determine their location by the size and shape of the waves. They also knew how to navigate using the stars. They could easily travel great distances by going from island to island. The Polynesians grew to accept sea travel as a way of life.
pages.brief: A map of the Pacific Ocean shows Asia, Australia, New Zealand, the Hawaiian Islands, Easter Island, and routes of Polynesian expansion. Early boats carry people safely between islands. By 1000 ce Polynesians live on nearly every habitable island they find. They navigate by wave size and shape and by the stars, and sea travel becomes a way of life.

pages.text: The Vikings More than 1,300 years ago, another group of people in another part of the world began to build larger boats. These people were the Vikings. They lived in the northern part of Europe. The Vikings were well known as warriors and conquerors. They were accustomed to traveling over water. By the year 700 ce, they were sailing boats that were superior to any others on the ocean. The boats they built, called knarrs (kuh-NARS), were used primarily for trading. These boats were up to 16.5 meters (54 ft) long and 4.5 meters (15 ft) wide. Because they were flat bottomed, the knarr boats could carry extremely heavy loads, and they were wide enough to carry a large amount of cargo. They were also very stable and could travel safely across the open ocean. At that time, most sailors did not like to lose sight of the coast, but the Vikings were fearless. They used a wooden dial called a sun compass to help them navigate and conquer new lands. They were the first Europeans to visit North America.
pages.brief: More than 1,300 years ago the Vikings live in northern Europe. They are known as warriors and conquerors. By 700 ce they sail knarrs, trading boats up to 16.5 meters long and 4.5 meters wide. Flat bottoms carry heavy loads, and the boats are stable on the open ocean. A wooden sun compass helps them navigate to North America.

pages.text: The Vikings also built warships known as longships. It often was difficult to tell if a longship was coming or going because they looked the same in the front and in the back. Because of the design of their longships, Viking attackers could easily change direction. Longships were able to travel as fast as 15 knots. (A knot is a way to measure speed on water. One knot is a little faster than one mile per hour.) Some of the larger longships carried as many as 200 warriors. The combination of large, speedy, easy-to-handle ships and a fierce fighting spirit made the Vikings tough to defeat. The Vikings ruled the ocean for nearly three centuries, but they did not improve on the design of the longship, and other nations eventually developed mightier ships. Viking knarr Viking longship.
pages.brief: The Vikings build warships called longships. Their front and back look the same, so it is hard to tell if one is coming or going, and attackers can change direction easily. Longships travel as fast as 15 knots and some carry 200 warriors. The Vikings rule the ocean for nearly three centuries, but other nations eventually develop mightier ships.

pages.text: Age of Discovery Until the 1400s, most sea explorers remained close to their home waters, but with the coming of the Age of Discovery, things changed dramatically. Every European sailing nation wanted to find new lands. The race was on, and the Americas were the prize. Shipbuilders searched for ways to build faster and safer ships. In the 1400s and 1500s, sea explorers used small, swift, sturdy ships known as caravels. These ships had three masts to hold sails. This design made the ships faster and easier to steer. Caravels had square sails on the fore and main masts, and a triangular-shaped sail, called a lateen, on the mast at the rear of the ship.
pages.brief: Until the 1400s most sea explorers stay near home waters. In the Age of Discovery, sailing nations race for new lands, with the Americas as the prize. Shipbuilders make caravels: small, swift, sturdy ships with three masts. Square sails on the fore and main masts and a triangular lateen sail at the rear make them faster and easier to steer.

pages.text: Consider the Conquered What impact did these discoveries have on the people already living in these places? Too often, the impact was a tragic one. Christopher Columbus, Hernan Cortes, and other Europeans who led these expeditions often exploited both the land and people they encountered. Their motive was usually financial gain. Before long, ships would also be used to carry people across oceans and enslave them far from their homes. Christopher Columbus sailed three of these ships. Santa Maria was the largest at 27.4 meters (90 ft) long and 9.1 meters (30 ft) wide. Compared to modern ocean liners and cargo ships, these ships were tiny—they didn’t even have cabins where the crew could sleep at night. Sailors just had to lie down on the deck or in the hold. But even though caravels were quite small, the famous explorer Ferdinand Magellan set out to sail five of these ships around the world with a crew of 260 sailors. Almost three years after they began the trip, Magellan’s crew returned. Only one of the ships and eighteen of the sailors made it around the world. The other ships were lost at sea, and the other sailors died. Magellan was not one of the survivors. He was killed somewhere in the Philippine Islands.
pages.brief: The impact on people already living in these places is too often tragic. Christopher Columbus, Hernan Cortes, and other Europeans exploit land and people for financial gain. Ships also carry enslaved people across oceans. Columbus sails three ships, including the 27.4-meter Santa Maria. Magellan sails five ships with 260 sailors; only one ship and eighteen sailors return.

pages.text: The Chinese While Europeans were sailing the world, the Chinese had also taken to the sea in another part of the world. By the 1400s, they were skilled sailors. Chinese people had long since invented the magnetic compass. They also invented the rudder a thousand years before Westerners. They used rectangular sails reinforced with strips of bamboo called battens. The battens made the sails sturdier and easier to furl and unfurl, and sailors could even climb them like ladders! From 1405 to 1443, the most famous Chinese explorer, Zheng He, traveled on seven long voyages with a fleet of sixty-two treasure ships. The Chinese called these ships junks. Inside the hull, the ship was divided into many sections, partitioned off with watertight walls or bulkheads to minimize potential damage. If the hull were breached, the leak could only flood a small section of the ship, rather than sinking the entire ship. Zheng He’s junks were much larger than European ships. His largest ship was so big that it could have held all three of Columbus’s ships on its deck. This massive ship was 121 meters (400 ft) long and 45.7 meters (150 ft) wide.
pages.brief: By the 1400s Chinese sailors are skilled. They invent the magnetic compass and use a rudder a thousand years before Westerners. Rectangular sails reinforced with bamboo battens are sturdier and easier to furl and unfurl. From 1405 to 1443 Zheng He travels on seven voyages with sixty-two treasure ships called junks. Watertight bulkheads limit damage if a hull is breached.

pages.text: In addition to the sixty-two main trading ships, more than a hundred smaller support boats were in the fleet. The Chinese sailed all the way to Africa to trade as well as to show the might of the Chinese empire to the rest of the world. Zheng He even carried a giraffe home to the emperor. War with their Asian neighbors caused the Chinese to turn their attention away from exploration, however. The emperor made ocean voyages illegal and had all the treasure ships destroyed. Chinese junk.
pages.brief: More than a hundred smaller support boats join the sixty-two main trading ships. The Chinese sail to Africa to trade and show the might of the Chinese empire. Zheng He carries a giraffe home to the emperor. War with Asian neighbors turns Chinese attention away from exploration. The emperor makes ocean voyages illegal and has all the treasure ships destroyed.

pages.text: Later Years As sea exploration continued, the Spanish led the way. By the 1500s, European shipbuilding had experienced vast improvements. The newest galleons, were comfortable. It took two trees to build one galleon. These vessels were as long as 42.7 meters (140 ft), but were still small compared to the Chinese ships. Many of them had nice, comfortable living quarters, at least for the officers. Galleons were dual-purpose ships that served as both trading vessels and warships. Because of their great size, these warships were capable of mounting many cannons, making them dangerous in battle. In the late 1700s, the British captain James Cook began some of the greatest explorations of his time. On his first ship, Endeavour, Cook sailed around the world.
pages.brief: As sea exploration continues, the Spanish lead the way. By the 1500s European shipbuilding improves greatly. Galleons are as long as 42.7 meters, with comfortable living quarters at least for officers. They serve as trading vessels and warships and can mount many cannons. In the late 1700s British captain James Cook sails around the world on his first ship, Endeavour.

pages.text: While many previous explorers sailed to make war or find treasure, Cook was interested in knowledge and science. He brought three scientists with him when he traveled, one astronomer (a scientist who studies the night sky) and two naturalists (scientists who study plants and animals). He also took many artists to document their discoveries. Cook observed the stars as he sailed, and whenever he came to a new land, he learned as much as he could about its plants and animals. His work broadened the European understanding of the world. Cook kept his crew healthy by making them eat foods such as limes and cabbages. Until Cook’s time, up to one-half of the crew on a long voyage would die of scurvy or other diseases. Cook knew his success as an explorer depended on keeping his crew in good health. Soon, all British sailors knew that they needed to eat vitamin C to survive. In the late 1770s, Cook visited Hawai ‘ i three times. On his last trip, in 1779, a fight broke out between the Hawaiians and Cook’s crew. Cook was killed.
pages.brief: Cook cares about knowledge. He brings three scientists, an astronomer and two naturalists, and artists to document discoveries. He learns about plants, animals, and stars in new lands. He keeps his crew healthy with limes and cabbages. In the late 1770s he visits Hawai‘i three times. On his last trip in 1779, a fight breaks out, and Cook is killed.

pages.text: Conclusion By the mid-1800s, sailors had explored and mapped most of the world’s coastlines. Very fast sailing vessels called clipper ships carried people across oceans in a matter of days. One clipper, Sir Lancelot, set a record by sailing from Australia to England in three months. Some of these ships had as many as thirty-five sails, and they could travel even in light breezes. By the 1870s, however, the steam engine largely replaced wind power. The Industrial Revolution swung into full gear, and machines became more significant to everyone. Bigger and faster ships than had ever been imagined suddenly became possible. Today, steam power is outdated, and ships run on different types of engines. Some submarines and aircraft carriers even run on nuclear power! Cruise ships carry thousands of people at a time like floating cities. When we look at some of the ships used by early explorers to sail across oceans, we have to admire the ingenuity of the people who designed those ships of discovery. While the impacts of sea exploration weren’t positive for everyone, setting sail into the unknown helped create the world we know today.
pages.brief: By the mid-1800s sailors have mapped most coastlines. Fast clipper ships carry people across oceans in days; one clipper, Sir Lancelot, sails from Australia to England in three months. By the 1870s steam engines largely replace wind power. Today submarines and aircraft carriers can run on nuclear power, and cruise ships carry thousands like floating cities. Early ships show ingenuity.

books.title: Seeing the Evidence: Forensic Scientists at Work
books.art_why: The keyword check flags cartoon, and the book mixes historical cases and named investigators rather than a straight modern photo subject.

pages.text: Introduction A man walked quickly across a field into an old mill, a building where wheat was crushed to make flour. Inside the building, he killed someone and then hurried away without being seen. Later, when police questioned the man, he insisted that he was innocent. This suspect might have gotten away with the crime if only he had wiped trace evidence off his shoes. Trace evidence is dust, hairs, threads, and other tiny bits of material found on or near a suspect or victim of a crime. When a detective named Edmond Locard used a microscope to study the man’s shoes, he noticed something no one else had seen: traces of flour on the heels and soles. This trace evidence matched the flour found at the mill where the victim was killed. This placed the man at the scene of the crime and helped to convict him of murder. Traces of flour could be seen on the suspect’s shoes with a microscope.
pages.brief: A man hurries across a field into an old stone mill where wheat is crushed into flour. Later, a detective in a white coat leans over a microscope, studying the man's shoes; pale traces of flour cling to the heels and soles, matching the flour inside the mill.

pages.text: Case File #1 Place: Oregon, U.S.A. Date: October 11, 1923 Crime: attempted robbery of a train known as the “Gold Special” Evidence: a pair of men’s overalls The Crime The scene of the crime is a remote stretch of railroad track in southern Oregon. The year is 1923. A Union Pacific freight train has been robbed. The bandits killed the engineer and two other train workers, and then used a homemade dynamite bomb to blow open the mail car. Back then mail often held valuable stock and bond certificates and sometimes cash or gold. When police searched the scene, the only piece of evidence they found was a pair of stained Union Pacific freight trains carried overalls that one of the all sorts of goods, including food and raw materials. bandits had left behind. Stop and Think! What could someone discover about you from examining your clothing?
pages.brief: A remote stretch of railroad track in southern Oregon, 1923. A Union Pacific freight train stands robbed, its mail car blown open by a homemade dynamite bomb. Beside the tracks, officers look down at a pair of stained overalls that one of the bandits left behind.

pages.text: Case Fact! The bandits stole a detonator from a construction site. They actually used too much dynamite and blew up any money that may have been in the mail car. The explosion also killed the Railway Post Office clerk. The explosion was so loud and destructive that the bandits ran from the scene without having robbed anyone of anything. Two men investigate dynamite and other explosive materials in 1924. How the Case Was Solved The police asked for help from Edward Heinrich, head of the Berkeley, California, forensic science laboratory. Heinrich was famous for being able to discover a great deal from very little evidence. Heinrich told the police to be on the lookout for a left-handed lumberjack in his early twenties weighing about 166 pounds (75 kg) and standing 5 feet 10 inches (1.8 m) tall. He also said the lumberjack had light brown hair, rolled his own cigarettes, and was unusually neat about his appearance.
pages.brief: A blast tears through the mail car, killing the Railway Post Office clerk, and the bandits run off with nothing. Nearby, two men in coats and hats examine dynamite and other explosive materials, turning the sticks over in their hands at a construction site in 1924.

pages.text: How could Heinrich have discovered all that from a pair of overalls? Heinrich explained: the fact that the left pocket was more worn than the right meant the owner was left-handed. What stained the overalls was sap from trees that grow in southern Oregon forests where lumberjacks work. The overalls’ size told Heinrich the lumberjack’s height and weight, and he could estimate the owner’s age from a light brown hair caught on a button. Tobacco shreds in a pocket and nail clippings caught in a seam told him the rest. And one more thing, Heinrich said, showing police a piece of paper he had found rolled up at the bottom corner of a pocket. The paper was bleached clean from many washings, but when treated with iodine, words began to appear. It was a receipt from a post office, made out to a man from Eugene, Oregon. Police went to the man’s house and learned that he was missing, along with his two brothers. Neighbors’ descriptions of the man matched Heinrich’s description exactly. When police tracked down the brothers several years later, they confessed to the robbery and murders and were sent to prison. The railroad robbers’ case was just one of some two thousand cases that Heinrich solved during his career as a forensic investigator.
pages.brief: Edward Heinrich holds up a pair of overalls for police, pointing to a worn left pocket, tree sap stains, and a light brown hair caught on a button. On the table lies a small bleached receipt he unrolled from a pocket corner and treated with iodine.

pages.text: Case File #2 Place: Anyplace, U.S.A. Date: anytime after 1950 Crime: a series of burglaries Evidence: dirty dishes The Crime Police thought that a series of burglaries had been committed by the same gang of thieves. When detectives finally located and raided their apartment, it was empty. The entire place had been wiped clean, except that the thieves had forgotten to run the dishwasher. How the Case Was Solved How could the police discover their identities? The secret was on the thieves’ hands. Look closely at the tips of your fingers and thumbs, and you will see raised ridges of skin running in patterns of curving lines: your fingerprints. Each of your fingerprints is different from the other nine, and each one is unique. No one else on Earth has fingerprints like yours, and no one ever will. In 1896, an Englishman named Edward Henry discovered a system to classify fingerprints. In 1901, he became a police commissioner and used his system to identify criminals.
pages.brief: Detectives step into an empty apartment, wiped clean, with one thing left behind: dirty dishes stacked inside the dishwasher. A close view shows the tips of fingers and thumbs, raised ridges of skin curving in patterns, each print different from all the others.

pages.text: Classifying Fingerprints Edward Henry based his system on features that every fingerprint shares. Every print has ridges (the raised lines) and furrows (the low spots between ridges). Prints also have arches, loops, and whorls. Arches are either tented (pointed at the top) or plain (rounded). Loops are either radial (running toward the thumb) or ulnar (running toward the little finger). Whorls are circular. Henry added smaller features—known as forks, dots, islands, hooks, and bridges—to his system. The type, number, and position of these features make each fingerprint unique. type 1 arch type 2 loop type 3 whorl Henry’s basic system is still used today. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has more than seventy million fingerprints in its database— the largest worldwide. Prints found at crime scenes can be compared quickly with all the prints in the databases. When a match turns up, police have a piece of evidence that places a person at the scene of a crime. Criminals are careful not to leave their fingerprints behind. In this case, CSIs got fingerprints from the dishes in the dishwasher and matched them to prints in the database.
pages.brief: A forensic examiner in a lab compares printed fingerprint cards, sorting them into three patterns: a pointed arch, a loop, and a circular whorl. Beside the cards, small features are marked where ridges fork, dot, and bridge on an enlarged print.

pages.text: What Is DNA? DNA is the part of each of your body’s cells that carries instructions that tell your body how to live and grow. About 98 percent of these instructions are the same in all people. The 2 percent that are different make your DNA unique, just like your fingerprints. Scientists can make microscopic X-ray pictures of unique DNA, known as DNA profiles. Just like fingerprint databases, police have developed computer databases of DNA profiles. DNA can be collected from almost any cell in your body, including cells in your hair, saliva, blood, sweat, and tears. DNA technology is so advanced that even a single skin cell could produce a DNA profile. Profiles can also be created using animal DNA. A database of cat DNA was started in Great Britain in 2013 to help establish that a cat hair found on a victim came from a particular suspect’s cat. DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder.
pages.brief: A scientist in a lab holds a vial beside a model of DNA shaped like a twisted ladder, and a glowing profile image of unique DNA. Nearby, samples of hair, saliva, and blood are laid out; even a single skin cell can produce a profile.

pages.text: Case File #3 Place: Indiana, U.S.A. Date: February 29, 2016 Crime: online sale turns to murder Evidence: a digital trail The Crime Not all evidence is tangible, or something that can be picked up, examined, and taken to the crime lab for testing. In many cases, the evidence comes in digital form. Emails, web searches, and GPS tracking information can all be used as evidence in court. One winter evening, Rito Llamas-Juarez and his family members answered an ad in an app where people connect to buy and sell their belongings. Llamas-Juarez found a listing advertising two cell phones for $500. His family contacted the person selling the phones, who used the name “Sports.” They arranged to meet in a parking lot. Three men approached Llamas-Juarez and his family members. One of the men shot and killed Llamas-Juarez, before fleeing the scene. Stop and Think! How could a digital trail help lead investigators to the suspect?
pages.brief: A winter evening in an Indiana parking lot. Rito Llamas-Juarez and his family stand beside their car, waiting to buy two cell phones advertised for five hundred dollars. Three men approach them across the asphalt, and one raises a gun.

pages.text: How the Case Was Solved Crime scene investigators searched the scene and discovered a smoked cigarette. They also found a cell phone box from the botched sale in Llamas-Juarez’s car. Investigators searched the phone Llamas-Juarez’s family used to arrange the sale. Police obtained a warrant to make the app used in the sale reveal the name of the owner of the Sports account. It was connected to a social media account that belonged to Larry Thomas. Once investigators had a suspect, they obtained a warrant to search his home. They discovered ammunition that was an exact match for the type used in the murder. Investigators swabbed Thomas for his DNA, and it matched the DNA found on the cigarette. They also matched the fingerprints discovered on the box to Thomas. In addition to physical evidence, investigators had digital evidence. They searched Thomas’s cell phone and found the password connected to the Sports account. Further, Thomas had emails from other potential buyers. Other key pieces of evidence included a photo of Thomas posing with the type of gun used in the shooting. Thanks in a large part to forensic digital investigators, Thomas was found guilty of his crimes.
pages.brief: Crime scene investigators photograph a smoked cigarette on the ground and lift a cell phone box from the car. Later, detectives study a phone, swab a suspect's cheek, compare ammunition, match fingerprints on the box, and look at a photo of the suspect posing with a gun.

pages.text: DNA Profiling Scientists use DNA to make a DNA profile for a specific, but unknown, suspect. Then they try to find a match— although it might take years. Police have a database where they can search DNA profiles of people involved in other crimes. People can also voluntarily upload their DNA to genealogy websites to find out information about their ancestors and locate unknown family members. Some genealogy websites allow law enforcement to upload crime scene DNA to search for matches. This new field of forensic science is called investigative genetic genealogy. Matches aren’t always exact, but rather allow investigators to close in on families with ties to the DNA sample. Investigators trace family trees connected to the DNA, and use clues such as age, gender, and known locations to determine their suspect. To confirm their suspicions, investigators need a DNA sample, often obtained from unknowing suspects in the form of a used straw or coffee cup from a suspect’s trash. DNA is not only used to convict suspects, but also to free wrongly convicted suspects. Investigators are now finding out that many convicted criminals, some serving lengthy or even life sentences, are not the real perpetrators. pages.text: Conclusion Each of the cases in this book explores a different kind of forensic evidence. There are other kinds of forensic evidence, too—footprints, shoe prints, palm prints, lip prints, bite marks, paint chips, tire tread marks, the markings on a bullet, and more. Any of these can link suspects to the scene of a crime or can show who is innocent. Together, the law enforcement officers and scientists who gather and study forensic evidence use virtually all of the sciences, from anthropology to zoology, in their work. Whatever science they specialize in, they all have one thing in common—they use their knowledge to see what goes unnoticed by the rest of us. vehicle identification number.
